summary: Albania replaced its 2008-era framework (Law 9887) with Law No. 124/2024 'On Personal Data Protection', approved by Parliament on 19 December 2024, published in January 2025 and in force from early 2025. The new law fully aligns Albania with the EU GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive, a milestone in its EU accession path. It applies to controllers and processors established in Albania and, GDPR-style, to foreign entities targeting or monitoring people in Albania.

The law imports the familiar GDPR toolkit: legal bases for processing, data subject rights, records of processing (replacing the old notification-to-the-Commissioner system), data protection impact assessments, 72-hour breach notification, and mandatory DPOs for public bodies and large-scale or sensitive processing. Cross-border transfers follow an adequacy-plus-safeguards model, with Standard Contractual Clauses and Binding Corporate Rules available and Commissioner authorisation as a fallback.

Enforcement sits with the long-established Commissioner for the Right to Information and Personal Data Protection (IDP), elected by Parliament for a seven-year term. Sanctions jumped dramatically from the old regime: fines can now reach ALL 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Businesses that were compliant under the 2008 law should treat this as a fresh GDPR-grade compliance exercise; the Commissioner has signalled a shift from awareness-raising to active enforcement.

summary: Algeria enacted Law 18-07 in June 2018, but the law only became effectively applicable in August 2023, one year after its supervisory authority, the ANPDP, was installed in August 2022. The law applies to public and private controllers processing personal data in Algeria and follows the classic Francophone model of prior declarations to the authority, with authorizations required for sensitive categories.

A major amendment, Law No. 25-11 of 24 July 2025, moved Algeria significantly closer to GDPR-style accountability: it makes appointing a Data Protection Officer mandatory, requires records of processing activities, logging, data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, prior consultation with the ANPDP, and introduces a breach-notification duty — the ANPDP must be notified within five days, and data subjects informed where the breach poses a high risk.

Cross-border transfers are permitted only to countries ensuring adequate protection, otherwise requiring ANPDP approval or a listed exception such as consent, contract performance or public interest. Enforcement combines administrative measures (warnings, formal notices, withdrawal of declarations/authorizations) with criminal penalties — fines of DZD 20,000 to 1,000,000 and imprisonment from two months to five years. Enforcement practice is still young: the authority has only been operating since 2022–2023 and is building out its supervisory activity.

summary: Andorra's Qualified Law 29/2021 on Personal Data Protection (LQPD), adopted 28 October 2021 and in force since 17 May 2022, replaced the 2003 law and deliberately mirrors the GDPR in structure and substance: same principles, data subject rights, accountability tools (records of processing, DPIAs, DPOs) and 72-hour breach notification. Implementing regulations for the law and for the supervisory agency were approved in 2022.

The supervisory authority is the Andorran Data Protection Agency (APDA), an independent body that also issues guidance on cookies and emerging topics such as AI. A key commercial point: Andorra has held an EU adequacy decision since 2010, reaffirmed in the European Commission's January 2024 review of pre-GDPR adequacy decisions, so personal data can flow freely from the EEA to Andorra.

The main divergence from the GDPR is the sanctions regime: fines are far lower than GDPR levels, topping out at €100,000 for very serious infringements. The LQPD treats EEA states, EU-adequate jurisdictions and Convention 108+ parties as safe destinations for onward transfers, and requires parental authorisation for consent-based processing of data of minors under 16.

summary: Angola's Law No. 22/11 of 17 June 2011 (Lei da Protecção de Dados Pessoais) is a Portuguese-inspired, pre-GDPR statute that remains the country's primary data protection law. Its central mechanism is regulatory gatekeeping: virtually all processing must be either notified to or authorized in advance by the Agência de Protecção de Dados (APD), which must decide on notifications within 30 days. Transfers abroad — including use of cloud servers outside Angola — require APD authorization and an adequacy assessment, with exceptions for express written consent, international treaties, contract performance and humanitarian purposes.

Although the law dates from 2011, the APD only became truly active in recent years and is now one of the busier enforcement stories in Lusophone Africa: it has issued fines including a USD 150,000 penalty against a telecoms provider for failing to notify multiple processing activities, and its published penalty bands run from roughly USD 7,000–15,000 for notification failures to USD 75,000–150,000 for major violations. In October 2024 it issued Instruction 02/APD/2024 addressing the duty to notify data breaches, partially filling a gap in the original law, which contains no general breach-reporting mechanism.

For companies in Angola's oil, banking and telecoms sectors, the practical priorities are inventorying processing activities and regularizing notifications/authorizations with the APD — the enforcement pattern so far punishes failure to file more than substantive processing conduct. The law has no DPO requirement and no modern accountability tooling, and reform discussions to modernize the 2011 framework are worth monitoring.

summary: Armenia's Law on Protection of Personal Data (HO-49-N), adopted 18 May 2015, is a comprehensive, Convention 108-inspired framework covering both public and private sector processing. It rests on familiar principles — lawfulness, purpose limitation, proportionality and consent as the default legal basis — and grants data subjects rights of access, rectification and erasure. Supervision sits with the Personal Data Protection Agency (PDPA), a unit of the Ministry of Justice rather than a fully independent regulator, which maintains a register of processors and must be notified before biometric or special-category data are processed.

The regime is lighter than the GDPR: there is no data protection officer requirement, registration is largely voluntary, and there is no general obligation to report breaches to the Agency (though data subjects must be informed of violations within three working days). Cross-border transfers are free to countries deemed adequate; transfers elsewhere need the Agency's prior written permission based on contractual safeguards it approves.

Enforcement has historically been modest, with administrative fines under the Code of Administrative Offences that are small by international standards. The PDPA became noticeably more active from 2024, launching a public-facing website with guidance, templates and training. Armenia has been discussing modernization — including a draft Cybersecurity Law pending in 2025 and moves toward closer GDPR alignment — so material change is plausible in the near term.

summary: Austria applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by the Datenschutzgesetz (DSG), whose Section 1 uniquely enshrines data protection as a constitutional right with direct third-party effect — a feature that predates and survives the GDPR. The DSG fills member-state discretion areas: it lowers the digital consent age to 14, sets detailed rules on image processing and video surveillance, protects DPO confidentiality, and adds criminal penalties for intentional data misuse.

The supervisory authority is the Datenschutzbehörde (DSB) in Vienna, which handles a heavy complaint caseload — Austria's active privacy litigation culture (home of noyb and Max Schrems) keeps it busy. Austrian enforcement has produced significant fines, including EUR 16 million against Austrian Post for profiling political affinity data and EUR 8 million against Rewe International, and Austrian complaints have driven landmark EU-level rulings on tracking and international transfers.

Practical compliance is standard GDPR — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, DPOs where triggered — with Austrian specifics around video surveillance, employee data (works council involvement), and the age-14 rule for information-society services.

summary: Azerbaijan's Law on Personal Data (No. 998-IIIQ of 11 May 2010) governs the collection, processing and protection of personal data by state bodies and private operators. It predates the GDPR era and uses its own vocabulary — 'owners' and 'operators' of personal data rather than controllers and processors — and centres on data subject consent, with rights to be informed, access, rectify and erase data. Personal data information systems must be registered with the state, subject to exemptions.

There is no standalone data protection authority. Supervision is exercised primarily by the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport, with enforcement roles shared by other bodies including the Ministries of Internal Affairs and Justice and the State Security Service — an arrangement that leaves oversight fragmented. The law has no DPO requirement and no general breach notification duty; cross-border transfers largely turn on the data subject's written consent.

In practice, enforcement of data protection rules is limited, and commentators have criticized Azerbaijan for prioritizing cybersecurity and information-control measures over individual privacy. Penalties for violations arise under the Code of Administrative Offences and the Criminal Code but active administrative enforcement is rare, so the compliance burden for businesses is more about registration formalities and consent paperwork than regulator scrutiny.

summary: Belarus's first comprehensive privacy statute, Law No. 99-Z of 7 May 2021 on Personal Data Protection (PDPL), entered into force on 15 November 2021. Broadly inspired by the GDPR and Russian-style data laws, it applies to state bodies, legal entities and individuals ('operators') processing personal data by automated or structured manual means, establishes consent as the primary legal basis with a closed list of exceptions, grants data subjects rights of access, correction, deletion and withdrawal of consent, and requires operators to adopt legal, organisational and technical protection measures, including a designated internal-control person or unit, staff training, and a published processing policy.

Supervision belongs to the National Personal Data Protection Center (NPDPC), created by Presidential Edict No. 422 of 28 October 2021 and operational since 15 November 2021. The NPDPC handles complaints, conducts inspections, approves cross-border transfers to countries lacking adequate protection (adequacy is generally recognised for Convention 108 parties and EAEU members), and issues clarifications. Breaches of protection systems must be reported to the NPDPC immediately and no later than three business days.

Enforcement runs through the Administrative Offences Code (Arts. 23.7, 24.11), with fines that are modest by GDPR standards — up to around 200 base units — plus criminal liability under Arts. 203-1 and 203-2 of the Criminal Code carrying up to three years' imprisonment for intentional unlawful collection or dissemination. Compensation for moral harm is available without proof of material loss. Belarus holds no EU adequacy decision, so exports of EU personal data to Belarus require SCCs or another GDPR transfer mechanism.

summary: Belgium applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by the Law of 30 July 2018 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data, in force since 5 September 2018, which replaced the 1992 Privacy Act. The 2018 law exercises the GDPR's opening clauses — most notably lowering the children's online consent age to 13, regulating processing of sensitive and judicial data, and transposing the Law Enforcement Directive — while a separate Law of 3 December 2017 created the supervisory authority.

That authority, the Autorité de protection des données / Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit (APD/GBA), succeeded the former Privacy Commission on 25 May 2018 and operates from Brussels with distinct inspection and litigation chambers. It has produced influential EU-level case law, including major decisions on the IAB Europe TCF consent framework used in online advertising, and its decisions are appealable to the Brussels Market Court, which regularly refines them.

Compliance is standard GDPR practice with Belgian specifics: multilingual transparency (Dutch/French/German), the 13-year consent age, camera-surveillance rules interacting with the separate Camera Act, and sectoral committees governing access to government databases. Enforcement is complaint-driven and moderately active, with fines typically in the tens to hundreds of thousands of euros.

summary: Benin's data protection regime sits inside its Digital Code — Law No. 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, amended by Law No. 2020-35 of 2021 — one of Africa's most sophisticated unified technology statutes, covering data protection alongside e-commerce, e-signatures, electronic communications and cybercrime. The personal data book of the Code is heavily GDPR-inspired, with accountability duties, processing registers, DPOs and breach notification.

The supervisory authority is the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles (APDP), created by Article 462 of the Code to replace the former CNIL-Bénin, governed by an 11-member board. Controllers must notify the APDP of most processing (small and medium enterprises are exempt unless processing is risky or sensitive), and DPO appointment — mandatory for state bodies and large-scale or monitoring-based processing — exempts an organisation from the notification duty, an unusual incentive design.

Penalties reach XOF 50 million for a first offence and XOF 100 million or 5% of annual sales for repeat offences within five years. The APDP is among the more active West African regulators, publishing communiqués, deliberations and compliance deadlines; foreign providers serving the Beninese market should take notification/DPO obligations and transfer adequacy requirements seriously.

summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina replaced its outdated 2006 Data Protection Law with a new, GDPR-aligned Law on the Protection of Personal Data, adopted by the Parliamentary Assembly on 30 January 2025, published in the Official Gazette of BiH No. 12/2025, in force from March 2025 and applicable from 4 October 2025. The reform transposes the concepts and structure of both the GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive and is a key step in the country's EU accession alignment.

The new law introduces GDPR-style data subject rights, mandatory Data Protection Officer appointments, Data Protection Impact Assessments, uniform rules on international transfers, and 72-hour breach notification to the strengthened Personal Data Protection Agency (AZLP). Penalties jump dramatically from the old law's token fines to GDPR-level exposure — up to 4% of global annual turnover or BAM 40 million per authoritative summaries.

As of August 2026 the law is fully applicable, but enforcement practice under the new regime is still young: the AZLP is building capacity and issuing guidance, and organisations that were compliant only with the 2006 law face substantial uplift work. Bosnia and Herzegovina does not hold an EU adequacy decision.

summary: The recorded law needs updating: Botswana repealed the never-fully-effective Data Protection Act 32 of 2018 and replaced it with the Data Protection Act 18 of 2024, assented on 29 October 2024 and brought into force on 14 January 2025. The new Act is significantly closer to the GDPR, with detailed duties for controllers, processors and sub-processors, dedicated children's-data provisions, and expanded powers for the Information and Data Protection Commission (IDPC).

Distinctive features include GDPR-scale sanctions — fines up to BWP 50 million or 4% of global turnover — 72-hour breach notification to the IDPC, mandatory DPOs (whose details must be registered) for large-scale monitoring or sensitive processing, and a soft data-localisation rule requiring that a copy of personal data transferred abroad be retained in Botswana during processing.

Enforcement is ramping up rather than mature: the IDPC is the independent supervisor and has been building out its compliance programme, but the Act has been fully effective only since January 2025 and published enforcement actions remain limited. The 2018 Act's history (its commencement was postponed by successive ministerial orders) is a reminder to verify commencement instruments when assessing Botswana.

summary: Bulgaria is an EU member state where the GDPR applies directly. The national Personal Data Protection Act (originally 2002) was substantially amended in 2019 to implement the GDPR's member-state options and transpose the Law Enforcement Directive. Bulgaria lowered the child consent age for information society services to 14 and added national rules on employment-context processing, such as limits on copying identity documents and retention of job applicant data (6 months by default).

The supervisory authority is the Commission for Personal Data Protection (CPDP), a five-member collegial body with its own budget and staff. The CPDP was an early mover on large GDPR fines: in 2019 it imposed roughly EUR 2.55 million on the National Revenue Agency for a massive breach caused by inadequate security measures, and it continues to issue significant penalties alongside a high volume of complaint decisions.

One distinctive episode: in late 2019 Bulgaria's Constitutional Court struck down the amendment's ten-criteria balancing test for journalistic processing as unconstitutional, so freedom-of-expression balancing is now assessed case by case. For businesses, compliance is standard GDPR compliance plus the Bulgarian employment-law specifics and the age-14 consent rule.

summary: Burkina Faso replaced its 2004 data protection law with Law No. 001-2021/AN of 30 March 2021, a substantially more modern and more coercive statute. The reform expanded definitions, created new data-subject rights, tightened rules on health data and international transfers, institutionalised data protection officers in public and private organisations, and significantly increased penalties — with administrative fines now calculated at 1% to 7% of the offender's turnover.

The supervisory authority is the Commission de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CIL), an independent administrative authority operational since 2007 and strengthened by the 2021 law, including provisions on cooperation with other data protection authorities. Controllers must file prior declarations with the CIL before processing, and obstruction of the CIL is itself punishable with fines of FCFA 5–10 million.

Enforcement reality: the CIL is genuinely active — running declaration campaigns, training DPOs and publicising the law — but operates in a difficult security and political context following the 2022 coups. Businesses operating in Burkina Faso should treat the declaration duty and turnover-based fine exposure as real, while expecting guidance to continue developing.

summary: Burundi's status has changed: after years with no comprehensive privacy statute, the National Assembly unanimously adopted a personal data protection bill on 15 January 2026, and Law No. 1/03 of 10 March 2026 on the protection of personal data was promulgated in March 2026. The law, structured in eight chapters, is now Burundi's primary hard law on personal data. It grants data subjects rights to information, access, correction, erasure, portability and objection, regulates automated decision-making, requires stronger controls (including impact assessments) for higher-risk processing, and covers data transfers and breach notification. The Ministry of Interior sponsored the legislation, citing the digitised voter register, expanding e-government and the planned biometric national ID as drivers.

The law creates an independent administrative authority to oversee data protection, but the authority's missions and organisation are left to a later decree, and no supervisory body is operational yet. Sanctions for breaches are provided in the law and sit alongside the Penal Code, the 2022 Cybercriminality Law and sectoral confidentiality rules (banking, health, labour).

Enforcement reality: this is a brand-new regime with no regulator constituted, no implementing decrees and no track record. Businesses operating in Burundi should monitor the establishment of the authority and treat detailed compliance parameters (deadlines, fines, registration mechanics) as not yet settled. Detailed English-language analysis of the text is still scarce.

summary: Cabo Verde was the first African country to enact comprehensive data protection legislation with Law No. 133/V/2001 of 22 January 2001. The framework was reformed in 2013 (Law 41/VIII/2013, which restructured the supervisory regime) and substantially modernized by Law No. 121/IX/2021 of 17 March 2021, which pulled the regime toward GDPR standards: unambiguous affirmative consent, extraterritorial application to foreign controllers processing data of people in Cabo Verde, a 72-hour breach notification duty, and conditional DPO appointment requirements.

The supervisory authority, the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (CNPD), operational since 2015, receives processing notifications, authorizes special-category processing, handles complaints and imposes sanctions. Cross-border transfers to countries without adequate protection are permitted only with CNPD permission, data subject consent, or specified necessity grounds.

The 2021 amendment sharply raised the stakes on enforcement, with first-offence fines ranging from CVE 1 million up to CVE 100 million. For a small island economy with growing outsourcing and tourism-related data flows, Cabo Verde now has one of the more modern regimes in West Africa on paper, though public enforcement actions remain relatively rare.

summary: Cameroon's status has changed: the long-pending bill became Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024 relating to Personal Data Protection, the country's first comprehensive data protection statute and the 38th in Africa. It protects the data of Cameroonian nationals and residents — and, unusually, extends to individuals transiting through Cameroon. The law imports many GDPR concepts: data portability, data protection impact assessments, records of processing, breach notification, DPOs and rules on cross-border transfers.

Two features stand out. First, breach notification must be made 'immediately' to both the Authority and affected data subjects, and the duty binds processors as well as controllers — stricter on paper than GDPR's 72-hour, controller-centric rule. Second, the law creates a new supervisory body, the Personal Data Protection Authority, but that authority is still being stood up, so day-one supervision is limited. Companies were given an 18-month transition that expired on 23 June 2026, meaning compliance is now formally due.

Enforcement exposure is potentially severe — commentary points to fines reaching XAF 1 billion and personal liability, including prison, for executives. With the transition period over but the Authority and implementing regulations still maturing, the practical enforcement environment in mid-2026 remains in flux. No EU adequacy decision exists.

summary: The Central African Republic enacted its first comprehensive data protection statute, Law No. 24.001 on the Protection of Personal Data, in January 2024 — a significant correction to older references that list the country as having no law. The text is comparable in structure to other modern francophone African laws: processing principles, data-subject rights, a mandatory in-country Data Protection Officer, breach reporting, and turnover-based administrative penalties of up to 5% of annual turnover.

Institutionally, the law provides for an independent supervisory authority to be established under the Ministry of Digital Economy, Posts and Telecommunications within 12 months of enactment; until it exists, the Ministry oversees implementation. Enforcement reality should be treated as embryonic: there is no operational regulator, no published guidance, and the country's security situation limits state capacity. Distinctive features to note in compliance planning are the residency requirement for the DPO and parental consent for processing minors' data.

summary: Chad's Law No. 007/PR/2015 of 10 February 2015 establishes a comprehensive framework for personal data protection, part of a 2015 package of digital laws that also created the supervisory body. Unusually, supervision is not vested in a dedicated privacy authority but in the cybersecurity regulator: the Agence Nationale de Sécurité Informatique et de Certification Électronique (ANSICE), established by Law No. 006/PR/2015. After years of latency, ANSICE became fully operational in late 2020 and has since begun data controller registration and enforcement activity.

The law applies to businesses of all sizes processing data of people in Chad. There is no country-wide registration system as such, but any processing must be declared in writing to ANSICE, and prior authorization is required for genetic and biometric data and health-sector research. Cross-border transfers require informing ANSICE beforehand; transfers to countries outside the CEMAC/CEEAC zones are allowed only where the controller ensures sufficient protection of the data subject's rights. The Act contains no DPO requirement.

Sanctions combine fines of XAF 1 million to 10 million with imprisonment of three months to one year for offenders. Enforcement is real but modest — ANSICE's dual cybersecurity/privacy mandate and limited resources mean compliance pressure in Chad is lower than in Africa's larger markets, though registration and transfer formalities are actively administered.

summary: China's Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), in force since 1 November 2021, is a GDPR-inspired but distinctly Chinese regime that applies to processing of personal information inside China and extraterritorially to handlers targeting or analyzing individuals in China. It sits atop a broader stack — the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and the Network Data Security Management Regulation effective 1 January 2025 — and is enforced principally by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) alongside MIIT, public security and market regulators. Consent (often 'separate consent' for sensitive data, transfers and disclosures) dominates the legal bases, and data of minors under 14 is treated as sensitive.

Its most distinctive feature is the cross-border transfer regime: exports of personal information must go through a CAC security assessment, a filed Chinese standard contract, or third-party certification — the last route completed by certification measures effective 1 January 2026 — with exemptions for low-volume, non-sensitive transfers (up to 100,000 individuals a year). Handlers above thresholds must appoint a personal information protection officer, conduct personal information protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, and foreign handlers caught extraterritorially must designate a local representative.

Enforcement is real and escalating: fines reach RMB 50 million or 5% of the prior year's turnover (the DiDi case exceeded RMB 8 billion), and a joint four-agency national enforcement campaign launched in March 2025 has specifically targeted cross-border transfer compliance, with published penalty cases through 2025-2026. Companies operating in or selling into China should treat PIPL compliance — especially transfer mechanisms and consent hygiene — as a board-level issue.

summary: Contrary to the recorded status, Comoros does have a comprehensive data protection law: the Union of the Comoros enacted its Law on the Protection of Personal Data on 29 June 2021. The text is closely modelled on the GDPR — it applies to automated and manual processing, has extraterritorial reach over foreign entities offering goods and services to, or monitoring, people in Comoros, and requires explicit consent or another legal basis for processing.

The law establishes a National Authority for the Protection of Personal Data as an independent public body with powers to issue warnings and administrative sanctions, and requires DPOs for public authorities and for large-scale monitoring or sensitive-data processing. Controllers must notify breaches to the Authority within 72 hours, and cross-border transfers follow a three-tier adequacy/safeguards/derogations structure.

The catch is enforcement: the Authority has never been formally constituted or made operational, so the law exists on paper with no active regulator, no adequacy decisions, no registration machinery and no published sanctions. Practically, organisations face a compliance framework without a supervisor — a common pattern in smaller African jurisdictions.

summary: The Republic of Congo (Brazzaville) adopted Law No. 29-2019 on the Protection of Personal Data on 10 October 2019, a comprehensive statute in the classic Francophone mold: lawful-basis requirements (consent, legal obligation, contract or other legitimate ground), prior declaration of processing to a supervisory authority, data subject rights, and tiered sanctions running from FCFA 8 million to 200 million, rising to 5% of annual turnover for the most serious harm. Private-sector entities were given one year and public bodies two years to come into compliance.

For years the law's main weakness was the absence of its regulator. That changed recently: after Council of Ministers approval in July 2024, Law No. 5-2025 of 29 March 2025 formally created the Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (CNPD), an independent administrative authority charged with authorizing and controlling processing, handling complaints, and sanctioning violations. The Commission is newly created and its operational machinery (registration portals, guidance, enforcement practice) is still in its infancy.

Practically, businesses operating in Congo should treat 2026 as the start of the enforcement era: the substantive obligations have been binding since 2020-2021, and a regulator now exists to enforce them. Companies handling sensitive or large-scale data should appoint a DPO and prepare declaration filings as the CNPD publishes its procedures.

summary: Côte d'Ivoire was an early West African adopter: Law No. 2013-450 of 19 June 2013 establishes a comprehensive regime for the processing and circulation of personal data, built on four pillars — legality, purpose (finalité), data minimization and consent. Data subjects have GDPR-style rights of access, objection (including to direct marketing), rectification, blocking and deletion, and a right not to be subject to purely automated decisions.

Distinctively, supervision is entrusted to the telecoms regulator: ARTCI is formally designated as the personal data protection authority, an independent administrative authority with regulatory, control and sanction powers. Most processing is subject to prior declaration, with authorizations for sensitive categories, under procedures fixed by Decree No. 2015-79. Appointing a data protection correspondent can relieve controllers of some declaration formalities.

Enforcement is real by regional standards — ARTCI runs compliance surveys, a permanent exchange framework with practitioners, and has issued significant sanction decisions; security failings can attract fines of up to XOF 10 million or up to 5% of pre-tax turnover. There is no EU adequacy decision.

summary: Croatia is an EU member state where the GDPR applies directly, supplemented by the Act on the Implementation of the General Data Protection Regulation (Official Gazette No. 44/2018), in force since 25 May 2018. The Implementation Act keeps the GDPR default consent age of 16 for children, and adds national rules on genetic and biometric data and detailed requirements for video surveillance — a distinctive Croatian focus that generates a steady stream of enforcement.

The supervisory authority is the Personal Data Protection Agency (AZOP), an independent body with over two decades of experience. AZOP has become one of the more active enforcers in Central and Eastern Europe: it imposed a record of roughly €10.5 million in fines across 97 decisions in 2024 and nearly €7 million during 2025, with significant penalties against debt-collection, retail and telecoms companies.

Practically, compliance in Croatia is GDPR compliance plus attention to the national video-surveillance regime (signage, retention limits, access controls) and biometric data rules. Organisations targeting Croatian consumers should treat AZOP as an authority with real teeth.

summary: Cyprus, as an EU member state, applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by Law 125(I)/2018 on the Protection of Natural Persons with regard to the Processing of Personal Data, enacted on 31 July 2018. The national law exercises the GDPR's member-state options and applies to controllers and processors established in Cyprus as well as foreign entities targeting or monitoring people there.

Cyprus's main national choices include setting the digital age of consent at 14 — below 14, processing based on a child's consent for online services is lawful only with parental authorisation — plus specific rules on combining genetic and biometric data and on processing for journalistic purposes. The standard GDPR obligations apply: 72-hour breach notification, DPOs where Article 37 triggers are met, records of processing, and Chapter V transfer mechanisms.

Enforcement rests with the Commissioner for Personal Data Protection in Nicosia, who can impose the full GDPR fine tiers on private organisations (up to EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover) and has issued a steady stream of decisions against banks, employers and marketers. As a small jurisdiction with a large financial and corporate-services sector, Cyprus sees particular regulatory attention on employee monitoring, direct marketing and international data flows.

summary: Czechia applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by Act No. 110/2019 Coll. on Personal Data Processing, effective 24 April 2019, which replaced the 2000 act and also transposes the Law Enforcement Directive. The Act's notable national choices are a children's online consent age of 15, exemptions and modifications for journalistic, academic and archival processing, and — most distinctively — a full waiver of administrative fines for public authorities and public bodies.

The regulator is the Office for Personal Data Protection (ÚOOÚ) in Prague, an independent authority dating to 2000. It runs annual inspection plans, handles complaints, and publishes opinions and annual reports; its fines are typically modest by Western European standards (thousands to low millions of CZK), though activity has been increasing, including in cookie-banner and telemarketing sweeps.

For businesses, compliance is standard GDPR work with Czech-language transparency, the 15-year consent age for online services, and awareness that public-sector counterparties face no fine exposure — political accountability and corrective orders are the enforcement levers there. The ÚOOÚ also acquired new roles in whistleblowing oversight and remains the contact point for cross-border EDPB cases.

summary: Denmark is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented by the Danish Data Protection Act (databeskyttelsesloven, Act No. 502 of 23 May 2018), which replaced the earlier Act on Processing of Personal Data from 25 May 2018. The Act exercises GDPR opening clauses on matters such as CPR (civil registration) numbers, employment data and sets the digital age of consent at the GDPR minimum of 13.

Denmark's most distinctive feature is its enforcement mechanics: because Danish constitutional tradition does not allow administrative authorities to impose punitive fines, Datatilsynet cannot fine directly. Instead it reports violators to the police with a recommended fine, and Danish courts impose the penalty through criminal proceedings — GDPR Recital 151 explicitly accommodates this. Serious violations can even carry up to six months' imprisonment. This makes headline fines rarer and slower than elsewhere in the EU (the largest court-confirmed fine to date is around DKK 1 million against Arp-Hansen Hotels), though Datatilsynet is highly active through orders, bans and influential guidance — including its prominent positions on Google Analytics and cloud services.

For organisations, day-to-day compliance is standard GDPR practice — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and transfer safeguards — with Danish specifics around CPR numbers and the court-based sanction route worth knowing before any enforcement encounter.

summary: Djibouti moved from having no data protection law to one of the region's most modern frameworks in a single step: the National Assembly adopted the country's first Digital Code (Code du Numérique, Law No. 019/AN/23/9ème L) on 30 June 2025, promulgated in July 2025. The Code runs to nearly 800 articles across eight books, with a 156-article data protection regime that is unmistakably GDPR-modelled — extraterritorial scope over foreign controllers targeting or monitoring people in Djibouti, 72-hour breach notification, DPOs, and turnover-based fines.

The law creates the Commission Nationale de Protection des Données Personnelles (CNDP) as an independent supervisory authority with administrative and financial autonomy, operating a tiered filing system: simple declarations for routine processing and prior authorisation for high-risk processing such as sensitive, genetic, biometric or criminal-record data. Administrative penalties reach DJF 70 million or 5% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher, with criminal penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment.

The critical caveat is institutional: the CNDP had not yet been operationally established as of the most recent reporting, so active enforcement has not begun and there is no regulator website or guidance yet. Local civil-society critics have also raised concerns about parts of the broader Code being used to restrict expression. Organisations touching Djiboutian data should begin aligning now, since the substantive obligations are already law.

summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo regulates personal data through its Digital Code, Ordinance-Law No. 23/010 of 13 March 2023 (published 11 April 2023) — an omnibus statute covering digital services, e-commerce, cybersecurity and, in Title III, a full personal data protection regime. This replaced a previously fragmented landscape and gives the DRC, for the first time, GDPR-inspired rules on lawful processing, data subject rights, and supervision, with the authority empowered to issue formal notices requiring violations to be remedied within as little as eight days.

The institutional side is the weak point. Articles 262–270 of the Code provide for a dedicated Autorité de Protection des Données (APD), but the Prime Ministerial decree needed to establish it has not been issued. Since a ministerial decree of August 2024, the APD's missions have been provisionally exercised by ARPTIC, the posts and telecoms regulator. The DRC also ratified the African Union (Malabo) Convention on cybersecurity and personal data protection, reinforcing its commitments.

For businesses this means the substantive obligations are law, but enforcement is transitional and guidance sparse: filings and interactions currently run through ARPTIC, penalty practice is undeveloped, and details such as breach deadlines and DPO thresholds are not yet well documented in accessible secondary sources. Companies in telecoms, fintech and mining services — the sectors most exposed — should monitor for the decree that will finally stand up the APD.

summary: Egypt's Personal Data Protection Law No. 151 of 2020 (in force since October 2020) created the country's first comprehensive framework, but it remained largely dormant for five years pending its Executive Regulations. That changed on 1 November 2025, when Prime Ministerial Decree No. 816 of 2025 issued the Executive Regulations and operationalized the Personal Data Protection Center (PDPC), under the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, as the licensing and enforcement authority. Compliance deadlines under the transition period ran into 2026, so 2026 is effectively year one of real enforcement.

The regime is notably permission-heavy compared with the GDPR. Controllers and processors need PDPC licenses or permits for regulated activities; cross-border transfers require a separate license or permit, an adequacy assessment of the destination, and the data subject's explicit consent. DPO appointment is mandatory and formalized — DPOs must be registered with the PDPC, meet qualification requirements and pass approved exams, and must file annual privacy reports. Breaches must be notified to the PDPC within 72 hours and to affected individuals within three working days. Children under 15 require documented written parental consent.

Sanctions combine administrative measures with criminal penalties, with fines ranging from EGP 100,000 to EGP 5,000,000 depending on the offense. Any business touching Egyptian personal data — including outsourcing, fintech and health sectors — should treat licensing, DPO registration and transfer permits as immediate 2026 priorities.

summary: Contrary to a common assumption that Equatorial Guinea has no data protection law, the country does have one on the books: Law No. 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data, a comprehensive statute available only in Spanish. It grants citizens the right to consent to the use of their personal data and to be informed and notified of any use of it, establishes general data protection requirements and data subject rights, and provides for penalties of up to FCFA 15 million for violations. The previously recorded status of 'no law' should therefore be corrected.

The critical caveat is enforcement: the law creates a supervisory authority — the Órgano Rector de Protección de Datos Personales — but that body has never been made operational. There is no functioning registration system, no published guidance, no enforcement track record, and very limited English-language analysis of the law's detailed provisions (transfer rules, breach duties and children's provisions are not clearly documented in accessible sources). In practical terms, compliance risk is low today but the legal obligations formally exist.

For a professional audience: treat Equatorial Guinea as a jurisdiction with a dormant law rather than a legal vacuum. Multinationals typically apply group-level standards, monitor for any move to stand up the authority, and note that the country participates in regional (CEMAC/African Union) discussions that could eventually revive implementation.

summary: Eritrea has no data protection legislation, no draft bill in progress, and no supervisory authority — it is one of the few African states with essentially no movement toward a data protection framework. There are no statutory duties around lawful basis, transparency, individual rights or breach reporting, and no complaint mechanism for individuals.

The only relevant texts are the unimplemented 1997 Constitution, whose Article 18 guarantees privacy of communications and correspondence but has never been brought into operative force, and the Communications Proclamation No. 102/1998, which regulates telecommunications, broadcasting and post under the Ministry of Transport and Communications rather than protecting personal data as such.

In practice, organizations processing data of Eritrean residents face no domestic compliance obligations, but also operate in an environment with pervasive state control of telecommunications and extremely low internet penetration. Any counterpart obligations will come from foreign law (e.g. GDPR extraterritoriality) rather than Eritrean law.

summary: Estonia is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented by the Personal Data Protection Act (isikuandmete kaitse seadus), adopted in December 2018 and in force since 15 January 2019. The Act covers the areas the GDPR leaves to member states — law-enforcement processing, journalistic and research exemptions, deceased persons' data — and sets the digital age of consent at 13. It also defines the mandate of the supervisory authority, the Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate (Andmekaitse Inspektsioon, AKI) in Tallinn.

Estonia's distinctive wrinkle is procedural: it has no general administrative-fine mechanism, so GDPR penalties of up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover are imposed through the national misdemeanour procedure. This long limited practical enforcement, and the Penal Code was amended on 1 November 2023 specifically to make the higher fine ceilings workable. AKI is nonetheless active through precepts, orders and guidance, in a country whose famously digital government (X-Road, e-residency) makes data governance a high-profile national topic.

For organisations, compliance is standard GDPR practice — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and Chapter V transfer safeguards — with the local nuance that formal fining runs through misdemeanour proceedings rather than pure administrative decisions.

summary: Eswatini's Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 5 of 2022) is a comprehensive, GDPR- and POPIA-influenced law that entered into force in 2022. It applies to data controllers and processors processing personal data by automated or non-automated means in Eswatini, whether or not they are domiciled or headquartered in the country. Rather than creating a standalone regulator, the Act designates the existing telecoms regulator, the Eswatini Communications Commission (ESCCOM), as the Eswatini Data Protection Authority (EDPA), with powers to investigate breaches, resolve complaints and sanction controllers.

Distinctive features include a statutory obligation for all entities that process personal data to register with the EDPA as controllers or processors, a 72-hour personal data breach notification duty, and sanctions ranging from warnings and enforcement notices to suspension of processing and fines of up to E5 million or 2% of annual turnover.

Enforcement is still maturing: ESCCOM/EDPA has been operationalising the regime through public notices and draft regulations (including on controller/processor registration and data protection officers), and there is not yet a significant published track record of fines. Companies dealing with Eswatini should treat registration and breach-notification readiness as the immediate compliance priorities.

summary: Ethiopia's first comprehensive privacy law, the Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, was approved by Parliament on 4 April 2024 and entered into force in mid-2024. It is broadly GDPR-inspired — lawful bases, data-subject rights, DPOs, 72-hour breach notification — but with distinctly Ethiopian features: a data-localisation requirement obliging controllers to store locally collected personal data on servers or data centres in Ethiopia, and prior regulator approval for cross-border transfers of sensitive data.

Supervision was assigned to the Ethiopian Communications Authority (ECA) rather than a standalone privacy regulator. The ECA maintains the register of controllers and processors, investigates complaints, issues enforcement notices and can impose administrative fines; the Proclamation also carries graduated criminal penalties, rising to five-to-ten years' imprisonment and fines of ETB 200,000–600,000 for unlawful international transfers. Minors are defined as under 16, and their data requires parental or guardian consent.

Enforcement reality lags the text: a year after entry into force, reporting described a slow path to operationalisation, with implementing directives, registration machinery and ECA capacity still being built. Companies serving the Ethiopian market should nonetheless plan for registration, DPO appointment, the localisation rule and the 72-hour breach clock, as the ECA has been holding implementation workshops and is expected to ramp up.

summary: Finland is governed directly by the GDPR, specified and supplemented by the national Data Protection Act (1050/2018), which entered into force on 1 January 2019 and replaced the earlier Personal Data Act. The Act exercises GDPR opening clauses on matters such as the processing of personal identity codes, journalistic and academic exemptions, and sets the digital age of consent at 13.

Supervision follows an ombudsman model: the Data Protection Ombudsman and their Office (tietosuoja.fi) act as the national supervisory authority. A distinctive Finnish feature is that administrative fines are not imposed by the Ombudsman alone but by a collegial sanctions board within the office, and public-sector bodies are exempt from administrative fines altogether — a notable divergence from many EU peers.

In practice, compliance in Finland is GDPR compliance: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and Chapter V transfer safeguards, with additional care needed around Finnish personal identity codes and employee data (governed by the separate Act on the Protection of Privacy in Working Life).

summary: France applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by the Loi Informatique et Libertés (Law 78-17 of 6 January 1978) — one of the world's oldest data protection laws, comprehensively rewritten in 2018-2019 to fit the GDPR. The national law fills the spaces the GDPR leaves to member states: it sets the digital consent age at 15 (with joint parent-child consent below that), keeps special regimes for health, biometric and criminal-record data, and preserves some prior formalities for sensitive health research processing.

Supervision belongs to the CNIL, the 1978-founded regulator that remains one of Europe's most influential authorities. The CNIL is a prolific enforcer, and notably uses the ePrivacy framework to fine cookie and tracker violations directly — bypassing the GDPR one-stop-shop — which has produced some of Europe's largest penalties against global tech platforms. It pairs enforcement with extensive practical guidance widely used across the French-speaking world.

For most organisations the compliance picture is standard GDPR: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPOs where required, and Chapter V transfer tools. The distinctive French angles are the age-15 rule for minors, strict CNIL cookie-consent doctrine, and active sectoral rules on health data hosting (HDS certification).

summary: Gabon's data protection framework rests on Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, one of Central Africa's earliest comprehensive statutes, originally modeled on France's pre-GDPR Informatique et Libertés regime: declaration and authorization formalities with a national commission, processing principles, data subject rights, and restrictions on transfers to countries lacking adequate protection. Its longtime regulator was the Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (CNPDCP).

In July 2023 the framework was significantly modernized by Law No. 025/2023, which amends the 2011 law to align more closely with GDPR-era standards. Key changes include transforming the CNPDCP into a strengthened Autorité pour la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel et de la Vie Privée (APDPVP) with enhanced powers, introducing specific protections for children's data, and setting financial sanctions ranging from FCFA 1 million to 100 million.

Enforcement reality is mixed: the authority has an established institutional history (it participates in the NADPA and AFAPDP regional networks) and the 2023 reform signals renewed political attention to the digital sector, but published enforcement actions are scarce and post-amendment implementing practice (breach notification mechanics, DPO expectations) is not yet well documented. Businesses in telecoms, banking and oil services should complete declaration formalities and watch for APDPVP guidance under the amended law.

summary: The Gambia enacted its first comprehensive privacy statute in 2025: the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act was passed unanimously by the National Assembly on 29 September 2025 and assented to by President Adama Barrow on 7 November 2025 — so the country has moved from 'bill in progress' to having a law in force. The Act was developed with Council of Europe support and aligns with GDPR-style international practice: lawful bases, data-subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, DPOs, and turnover-based fines up to 4% of annual global turnover.

Rather than creating a brand-new agency, the Act vests supervision in the existing Information Commission, established under the Access to Information Act 2021, giving it a dual access-to-information and data protection mandate with powers to investigate complaints, issue guidelines and impose administrative fines. Criminal sanctions range from GMD 500,000 for unlawful processing up to GMD 10 million and 10 years' imprisonment for aggravated offences such as unlawful data sales.

Distinctive points: children are defined as under 18 with parental consent generally required, cross-border transfers need adequacy or Commission-adopted safeguards with documented transfer assessments, and DPOs are mandatory for public authorities and large-scale monitoring or sensitive processing. Enforcement is nascent — the Commission is still standing up its data protection function — but the compliance clock has started for organisations processing Gambian data.

summary: Georgia's Law on Personal Data Protection (No. 3144, adopted 14 June 2023) replaced the 2011 law, with its main provisions in force since 1 March 2024. It is closely modelled on the GDPR and was a deliverable of Georgia's EU association agenda. The law applies to processing in Georgia and introduces GDPR-familiar machinery: legal bases, data subject rights, records of processing, mandatory DPOs for public institutions and organisations doing large-scale or sensitive-data processing, direct-marketing rules, and video surveillance provisions.

Breaches likely to cause significant harm must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours. Cross-border transfers follow an adequacy-based model, with safeguards or authority permission required for other destinations. Administrative fines are modest by European standards — GEL 1,000 to 10,000 depending on the offence, adjusted for the violator's turnover and aggravating or mitigating circumstances — though reputational and inspection risk is real, as the regulator has been an active inspector since 2024.

The big 2026 development is institutional: under a December 2025 amendment, the independent Personal Data Protection Service (PDPS) was abolished on 2 March 2026 and its supervisory functions transferred to the State Audit Office, as part of a broader restructuring that also dissolved the Anti-Corruption Bureau. The government frames the SAO as a constitutionally independent home for the function; critics see a weakening of dedicated data protection oversight. Organisations should watch how SAO enforcement practice develops and update any references to the PDPS in their documentation.

summary: Germany applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG), enacted in 2017 and effective alongside the GDPR on 25 May 2018. The BDSG uses the GDPR's opening clauses extensively: it lowers the DPO-appointment threshold (mandatory once 20 or more people regularly process personal data), adds detailed rules on employee data processing (§26 BDSG), credit scoring, and video surveillance, and each of the 16 Länder has its own state data protection law for its public sector.

Supervision is uniquely decentralised. The federal BfDI oversees federal public bodies and telecommunications/postal providers, while 17 independent state authorities (Landesdatenschutzbehörden) supervise the private sector and state public bodies — so a company's lead German regulator depends on where it is established. Coordination happens through the Datenschutzkonferenz (DSK), which issues joint guidance. German authorities are prolific enforcers, with landmark fines against H&M (€35m) and others, and German courts see heavy GDPR damages litigation.

For businesses, the German specifics that matter most are the low DPO threshold, strict works-council and employee-data rules, conservative positions on consent and tracking (reinforced by the TDDDG for cookies), and the need to identify the correct state authority. Enforcement culture is formalistic and complaint-driven, and audits are common.

summary: Ghana was an early African mover on data protection: the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) has been in force since October 2012 and established the Data Protection Commission (DPC), one of the continent's more active regulators. The Act applies to anyone processing personal data using equipment or a controller in Ghana, imposes eight data protection principles broadly modeled on pre-GDPR European law, and gives data subjects rights of access, correction and compensation. Its most distinctive operational feature is mandatory registration: every data controller must register with the DPC and renew every two years, and processing without registration is a criminal offence.

Enforcement is real but modest by modern standards — penalties are criminal fines (capped around GHS 60,000) and imprisonment rather than GDPR-style turnover-based administrative fines, and the Act lacks a fixed breach-notification deadline, a mandatory DPO, and a dedicated cross-border transfer regime. The DPC compensates with sustained registration and compliance campaigns, and in practice pushes larger controllers to designate data protection supervisors.

The framework is on the cusp of a major overhaul: a Data Protection Bill, 2025 would repeal and replace Act 843 with a far more stringent regime — turnover-linked penalties, detailed cross-border transfer rules with data-localization preferences (mandatory localization for children's, biometric, health and national-identity data), parental consent requirements, and rules on automated decision-making. As of mid-2026 the Bill was still being finalized for introduction in Parliament, so Act 843 remains the operative law for any near-term compliance discussion.

summary: As an EU member state, Greece is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented since August 2019 by Law 4624/2019, which implements the member-state derogations and transposes the Law Enforcement Directive. The combined framework applies to any organisation established in Greece and to foreign organisations offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Greece. Law 4624/2019 also carried over rules in areas like employee data processing, which is a well-litigated topic before the Greek regulator.

Greece's notable national choices include setting the digital age of consent at 15 (parental consent required below that for online services), specific conditions for processing employee data, and a EUR 10 million cap on administrative fines against public bodies. summary: Guinea regulates personal data through Law No. L/2016/037/AN of 28 July 2016, a hybrid statute whose first part deals with cybercrime and whose second part sets out a personal data protection regime. The data protection portion follows the francophone West African model inspired by the ECOWAS Supplementary Act: processing rests on express prior consent or another legitimate basis, data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and most processing is subject to a prior declaration filed with the supervisory authority before it can begin.

The law's biggest practical weakness is institutional. It provides for the creation of a national data protection authority, but a decade after enactment that authority has still not been effectively established, so the declaration regime, complaint handling and sanctions exist largely on paper. Businesses operating in Guinea should treat the substantive principles (consent, purpose limitation, security) as binding law, while recognising that active administrative supervision and enforcement are minimal in practice.

There is no EU adequacy decision, no operational registration portal, and little published enforcement history. Companies typically benchmark against the text of the 2016 law plus the ECOWAS framework, and monitor for the eventual establishment of the authority and implementing decrees.

summary: Guinea-Bissau has no data protection law and no supervisory authority, making it one of the very few ECOWAS member states without such legislation. It also lacks adjacent frameworks such as comprehensive cybercrime or electronic transactions laws, so there is no operative statutory regime governing how organisations collect or process personal data.

The main protections are constitutional and regional: the Constitution enshrines rights to privacy and, by extension, personal data protection, but without implementing legislation the direct applicability of these rights to data processing disputes is unclear. As an ECOWAS member, Guinea-Bissau is also covered in principle by the 2010 ECOWAS Supplementary Act on Personal Data Protection, though this has no practical domestic enforcement machinery.

Drafting of a national data protection law has reportedly been initiated, aiming to regulate processing and establish a legal and institutional framework, but as of mid-2026 no bill has advanced to enactment. Political instability — including the 2025 coup — makes near-term legislative progress uncertain. Businesses operating there typically apply regional or contractual standards voluntarily.

summary: Iceland applies the EU GDPR through the EEA Agreement, implemented and supplemented nationally by Act No. 90/2018 on Data Protection and the Processing of Personal Data, in force since 15 July 2018. The supervisory authority is Persónuvernd, an active, independent regulator based in Reykjavík that handles a high volume of complaints for a small jurisdiction and participates in EU-level cooperation as an EEA authority. summary: Iran has no comprehensive data protection law in force; a draft has been in progress for years without enactment. The best-known text is the Draft Bill on Protection of Data and Privacy in Cyberspace (2018), prepared by the ICT Ministry, and successor drafts of a Personal Data Protection and Safeguarding Bill have circulated through government and parliament (Majlis) since, but none has become law as of mid-2026. No national data protection authority exists.

In the meantime, privacy protection is scattered across sectoral and general instruments: the Electronic Commerce Law (2004) contains consent-based rules for personal data in electronic transactions; the Computer/Cyber Crimes Act (2011) criminalizes publishing another person's images, recordings or personal and family secrets without consent (61 days to 6 months' imprisonment or IRR 1-10 million fines); the non-binding Charter on Citizens' Rights (2016), the Law on Publication of and Access to Data (2010), the Constitution and Sharia principles round out the picture.

For businesses, there are no registration, DPO, breach notification or cross-border transfer requirements — but data practices intersect with Iran's heavy internet controls, localization pressures via the National Information Network agenda, and criminal exposure for wrongful disclosure. Sanctions considerations dominate any practical engagement. The draft bill's timetable remains unclear, and its passage would likely still leave enforcement in the hands of state bodies rather than an independent DPA.

summary: Iraq has no comprehensive data protection law in force and no data protection authority. Privacy protection rests on fragmented sources: the 2005 Constitution guarantees personal privacy (Article 17) and confidentiality of communications (Article 40), the Penal Code contains general privacy-related offences (e.g., disclosure of secrets), and the Civil Code offers general tort remedies. Sector-specific obligations exist mainly through Communications and Media Commission (CMC) directives and licensing conditions for telecom operators and digital platforms.

A draft Personal Data Protection Law — reportedly introduced to the Council of Representatives around 2021 and envisaging a national data protection authority — has been mentioned by several legal trackers, but it has not advanced visibly, has not been enacted, and reliable official documentation of its status is scarce. A long-running draft Cybercrime (Information Technology Crimes) Law and a draft Right to Information Act (2023) have drawn criticism for potential restrictions on expression and privacy rather than protections.

In practice, businesses processing Iraqi personal data face no registration, DPO, breach notification or transfer requirements under a general data law, but should observe CMC telecom/platform rules, contractual confidentiality, and Penal Code exposure for wrongful disclosure. The regulatory direction remains uncertain amid Iraq's broader legislative gridlock.

summary: Ireland is governed directly by the GDPR, given further effect by the Data Protection Act 2018, in force since 25 May 2018. The Act establishes the Data Protection Commission (DPC), sets the digital age of consent at 16 — the highest level the GDPR permits — and adds child-specific protections: a specific right to erasure for data collected from children online, and criminal offences for companies that process children's data for direct marketing, profiling or micro-targeting.

Ireland's outsized importance comes from the GDPR's one-stop-shop: because Meta, Google, Apple, TikTok, Microsoft/LinkedIn and many other multinationals have their EU headquarters in Dublin, the DPC is lead supervisory authority for much of Big Tech's European processing. Its decisions — often shaped by EDPB dispute-resolution — include some of the largest fines in GDPR history, most famously the €1.2 billion Meta transfer decision in 2023, giving the DPC an enforcement docket of global significance despite long-standing criticism from privacy advocates about pace.

For ordinary organisations, compliance in Ireland is standard GDPR compliance — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and Chapter V transfer safeguards — with particular care around children's data given the 16-year consent threshold and the DPC's Children's Fundamentals guidance.

The regulator, the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, is one of Europe's most assertive: it issued Europe's early landmark actions on generative AI (temporary limitation and fine against OpenAI/ChatGPT), fined Clearview AI, runs aggressive cookie and telemarketing enforcement, and treats age verification as a substantive compliance duty for online and AI services. summary: Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI), originally enacted in 2003 and substantially rewritten by amendments effective April 2022, is a mature, comprehensive privacy law applying to virtually all private-sector businesses handling personal information, with extraterritorial reach over foreign operators serving people in Japan. It is enforced by the independent Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). Japan holds an EU adequacy decision (2019, reaffirmed after review), operating a mutual adequacy arrangement with the EU — a distinctive 'data free flow with trust' posture Japan has championed globally.

The APPI is less prescriptive than the GDPR: no DPO mandate, no general registration, and a purpose-notification model rather than strict legal bases. Its sharpest teeth are the mandatory breach regime (report qualifying incidents to the PPC promptly, with a final report within 30 days, or 60 for malicious acts, and notify affected individuals), rules on third-party provision (traceability records and the opt-out filing system), pseudonymized/anonymized data categories, and cross-border transfer conditions requiring consent, an adequate destination, or safeguards plus detailed disclosures about the destination country's regime. Corporate fines reach JPY 100 million for order violations and database theft.

A significant amendment was enacted in 2026 as part of the APPI's triennial review: it introduces protections for minors under 16, extends improper-use and improper-acquisition prohibitions to 'contactable personally referable information,' and moves individual breach notification to a more risk-based approach; provisions will phase in over the coming years. The PPC enforces mainly through guidance, investigations and binding orders rather than headline fines, but compliance expectations — especially around breach reporting and transfers — are taken seriously by Japanese business.

summary: Kazakhstan's Law No. 94-V 'On Personal Data and Their Protection', in force since 2013 and amended repeatedly, is a consent-centric regime: collecting and processing personal data generally requires the data subject's consent unless a statutory exception applies. It applies to state bodies and private 'owners' and 'operators' of personal data databases, and is supplemented by ministerial rules on collection and processing. The authorized state body is the Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation and Aerospace Industry, which gained explicit oversight and enforcement functions through amendments in the early 2020s.

Kazakhstan's most distinctive features are data localization and, since 1 July 2024, rapid breach reporting. Personal data of Kazakh citizens must be stored in databases physically located in Kazakhstan — copies may be transferred abroad, but the primary database stays onshore. Cross-border transfers are permitted to jurisdictions ensuring adequate protection or with consent and other statutory grounds. Data breaches must now be reported to the Ministry within one working day of discovery, one of the shortest deadlines anywhere.

Enforcement historically leaned on the Administrative Offences Code, whose MCI-indexed fines are modest by international standards, with criminal liability reserved for serious unlawful collection or dissemination; regulators have signalled tightening oversight amid a string of high-profile leaks. There is no general registration or licensing of controllers, but organisations must designate a person responsible for data processing, adopt internal documentation, and destroy or depersonalise data once the purpose is fulfilled.

summary: Kyrgyzstan's Law No. 58 'On Personal Information' of 14 April 2008 was one of Central Asia's earliest data protection statutes, and it has been significantly modernized by amendments in 2017, 2021 and 2022. It regulates collection, processing and protection of personal data by public and private 'holders', built on consent or another lawful basis, purpose limitation, and data subject rights of access and correction.

A dedicated regulator — the State Agency for Personal Data Protection under the Cabinet of Ministers — was established in December 2021, giving the law an enforcement arm it previously lacked. Its flagship mechanism is mandatory registration: holders of personal data arrays must register with the Agency via a three-stage online process launched in November 2022 (currently workable mainly for local entities). summary: Lebanon's Law No. 81 of 10 October 2018 on Electronic Transactions and Personal Data (in effect since 31 March 2019) is the country's first legislation addressing personal data, but it is a hybrid statute — most of it concerns e-transactions, e-signatures, e-commerce and cybercrime, with one section devoted to personal data. Its most distinctive — and dated — feature is a licensing model: rather than an independent regulator, oversight sits with the Ministry of Economy and Trade, which issues permits and licenses for personal data processing where required. In practice broad exemptions (consent-based processing, employers processing employee data, businesses processing customer data for legitimate operations, public authorities, non-profits, schools) mean most routine processing needs no permit. The law contains no DPO requirement, no breach notification duty, and no dedicated cross-border transfer regime.

Enforcement has been minimal amid Lebanon's economic and institutional crisis, and civil society (notably SMEX) has criticized the law as falling well short of GDPR-style protection. Companies handling Lebanese data face light formal obligations, but should watch for reform proposals and note that sectoral rules (banking secrecy, telecom) can impose stricter duties than Law 81 itself.

summary: Lesotho enacted one of Southern Africa's earliest data protection statutes — the Data Protection Act, published in the Government Gazette on 22 February 2012 — making the recorded status of an in-force law correct. The Act applies to automated and manual processing, sets out familiar principles (minimality, purpose specification, security safeguards), treats children's data as sensitive personal information requiring parental consent, requires controllers to notify the Data Protection Commission before processing, and mandates breach notification 'as soon as reasonably possible' to the Commission and affected individuals. Its transfer rules are distinctive for privileging SADC member states that have transposed equivalent protections.

The fatal weakness is institutional: the Data Protection Commission the Act establishes has never been appointed. Fourteen years on there is no commissioner, no registration machinery, no guidance and no enforcement — local practitioners describe the law as having 'no teeth'. Even if constituted, the Commission's powers are weaker than modern peers; notably, it cannot impose administrative fines, leaving only limited criminal penalties.

Practically, organisations in Lesotho face a technically enforceable statute with zero supervisory activity, and reform advocates are pressing for a modernised law and an operational authority. Compliance is prudent (courts could still apply the Act, and enforcement could reach past conduct once a Commission exists), but there is no regulator to register with today.

summary: Liberia's status has moved from 'no law, no bill' to an active legislative process. The country still has no specific data protection law, but a draft Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act — 'An Act for the Collection, Processing, Transmission, Storage, Protection, and Use of Personal Information in Liberia' — was developed by the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications with Internews support under the EU-funded Liberia Media Empowerment Project.

As of August 2026 there is no confirmation of enactment, so the bill remains in progress.

In the interim, protections are fragmentary: constitutional privacy guarantees, plus sectoral instruments (telecommunications and cybercrime-related provisions). A 2025 UN review highlighted the gaps in Liberia's online rights framework, adding international pressure to complete the legislation. Organisations handling Liberian data should track the bill, which would create the country's first structured framework and supervisory arrangements for personal data.

summary: Libya has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. Privacy protection rests on scattered provisions: the Constitutional Declaration protects private life (Article 12) and the confidentiality of correspondence and communications (Article 13), and the 1953 Penal Code contains general protections for private correspondence and the home.

The closest things to modern data rules are sectoral and digital-economy statutes. Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions and Law No. 5/2022 on Combating Cybercrime introduce some data-handling and security obligations, though it remains unclear how far the Electronic Transactions Law binds private entities. In June 2025 the Central Bank of Libya issued Circular No. 18, a 'Data Protection System and Executive Regulation' creating data protection requirements specifically for the banking and financial sector — the most concrete data protection instrument in the country to date.

There is no supervisory authority for personal data; the National Information Security & Safety Authority (NISSA) handles information security rather than privacy enforcement. Organizations operating in Libya face contractual and sectoral obligations (especially in banking) rather than a general compliance regime, and no comprehensive bill was identified as pending as of mid-2026.

summary: Liechtenstein applies the GDPR through its EEA membership, supplemented by the national Data Protection Act (Datenschutzgesetz, DSG) enacted on 4 October 2018. Compliance obligations mirror the GDPR everywhere in the EEA: lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, DPO designation where triggered, and Chapter V transfer tools for exports outside the EEA. summary: Madagascar's Law No. 2014-038, adopted in December 2014 and promulgated on 9 January 2015, is a pre-GDPR, French-inspired data protection statute. It applies to automated and manual processing carried out wholly or partly on Malagasy territory, imposes classic principles (lawfulness, purpose limitation, accuracy, security, confidentiality) and relies on prior formalities — declarations and authorisations — rather than the accountability model of newer laws. It has no general breach-notification duty and limited children-specific rules.

The big development is institutional: for nearly a decade the law was a dead letter because its supervisor, the Commission Malagasy de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CMIL), did not exist. The CMIL was created by Decree 2023-1541 (December 2023), its members were sworn in before the Supreme Court on 4 August 2025, and it adopted its procedures manual in December 2025. It joined the francophone association of DPAs (AFAPDP) as a full member in November 2025, with operationalisation support from the OIF and AFAPDP.

Enforcement reality: the CMIL declares itself fully operational and holds both regulatory and sanctioning powers under the 2014 law, but it is a brand-new regulator with no enforcement track record, and the underlying statute is dated relative to GDPR-era peers. Expect guidance, registration mechanics and possibly a modernised law to develop over the next few years.

Enforcement is young: the framework is in place and MACRA has been standing up registration and guidance, but there is little published enforcement history yet. Penalty exposure under the Act is primarily criminal (fines and imprisonment) rather than GDPR-scale administrative fines.
