summary: Malta is an EU member state where the GDPR applies directly, supplemented by the Data Protection Act (Act XX of 2018, Chapter 586 of the Laws of Malta), in force since 28 May 2018, which repealed the previous Chapter 440 regime. The supervisory authority is the Information and Data Protection Commissioner (IDPC), appointed under Article 11 of the Act, which enforces both the GDPR and the national Act and also administers freedom-of-information functions. Given Malta's outsized iGaming, financial services and remote-services sectors, the IDPC's caseload skews toward complaints about online operators, employee monitoring and direct marketing. summary: Mauritania enacted Law No. 2017-020 on the Protection of Personal Data on 22 July 2017, a comprehensive statute in the Francophone declaration/authorization tradition establishing lawful-processing principles, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure) and a supervisory authority. Implementation lagged badly: the decree organizing the Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (APD) was only adopted in February 2022, and its members were sworn in later that year.

The APD is now functioning: it published a 2023–2026 strategic plan framed around bringing Law 2017-020 into effective application, signed a cooperation agreement with Algeria's ANPDP in October 2024, and joined the Global Privacy Assembly in November 2024. However, its enforcement track record is thin, and some secondary sources still describe the law as not yet fully effective in practice — the gap between the statute and day-to-day enforcement is the defining feature of the Mauritanian regime.

Companies operating in Mauritania should expect prior-formalities obligations with the APD and honor core data subject rights, but should verify current APD practice directly, as guidance, penalty practice, and detailed rules (breach notification, transfers, DPO expectations) are not yet well documented publicly.

summary: Mauritius's Data Protection Act 2017 (Act 20 of 2017), in force since early 2018, replaced the 2004 Act specifically to align with the GDPR and modernise one of Africa's oldest data protection regimes. It applies to controllers and processors established in Mauritius or using equipment there, covers the full set of GDPR-style principles and data subject rights, requires 72-hour breach notification to the Data Protection Commissioner, and sets a parental-consent age of 16 for children's data. Mauritius was the first African state to sign and ratify Council of Europe Convention 108 and its modernised 108+ protocol, underlining its position as a regional privacy leader.

Two features stand out for foreign businesses. First, registration is genuinely mandatory: every controller and processor must register with the Data Protection Office and renew its certificate every three years, and processing without registration is a criminal offence. Second, every controller and processor must designate a data protection officer. Cross-border transfers require Commissioner-approved safeguards, explicit consent or another statutory ground.

Enforcement is real but criminal-law flavoured: the Data Protection Office, an established and active regulator, investigates complaints and issues enforcement notices, with offences punishable by fines up to MUR 200,000 and imprisonment up to five years rather than turnover-based administrative fines. Mauritius does not hold an EU adequacy decision, though its Convention 108+ status and GDPR alignment ease practical transfer arrangements.

summary: Moldova is in the final weeks of a generational transition. The framework currently in force is Law No. 133 of 8 July 2011 on Personal Data Protection, a Convention 108/Directive 95/46-era law that requires controllers to register processing operations with the National Center for Personal Data Protection (CNPDP), observe lawfulness and proportionality, and respect data subject rights of access, rectification and objection. Enforcement under it operates through the Contravention Code, with modest fines — a recent published penalty was MDL 6,500 (about EUR 330).

On 25 July 2024 Parliament adopted Law No. 195/2024 on personal data protection, which substantially transposes the GDPR and becomes applicable on 23 August 2026 — this month. It replaces Law 133/2011 with GDPR architecture: accountability duties for controllers and processors, expanded data subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, DPO requirements, a GDPR-style transfer regime, and far heavier sanctions, ending the old registration model. The two-year transition period given to organisations is now effectively over.

Anyone dealing with Moldova today should treat Law 195/2024 as the operative benchmark: EU candidate-country alignment is driving convergence with the GDPR, and the CNPDP is repositioning as a GDPR-style supervisory authority. Moldova does not hold an EU adequacy decision, so transfers from the EU still need safeguards.

summary: Monaco comprehensively overhauled its data protection framework with Law No. 1.565 of 3 December 2024, which repeals and replaces the 1993 law (Law 1.165) and aligns the Principality with the GDPR and Council of Europe Convention 108+. The law has extraterritorial scope modelled on GDPR Article 3: it covers controllers and processors established in Monaco and foreign ones offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Monaco. Sovereign Ordinance No. 11.327 of 10 July 2025 set out the detailed implementing rules, and pre-existing processing benefits from a one-year transitional window.

The former Commission de Contrôle des Informations Nominatives (CCIN) has been replaced by the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles (APDP), which has substantially stronger powers, including administrative fines of up to €10 million or 4% of worldwide turnover. The law strengthens data subject rights (information, access, rectification, erasure, portability), introduces DPIAs for high-risk processing, mandatory records of processing, DPO designation for certain categories of organisations, and certification mechanisms.

The shift is from the old prior-formalities culture (declarations and authorisations to the CCIN) to a GDPR-style accountability model. Monaco does not hold an EU adequacy decision, so EEA exporters still need safeguards to send data to Monaco, though the 2024 reform is widely seen as positioning Monaco for a future adequacy bid.

summary: Mongolia's Law on Personal Data Protection was adopted on 17 December 2021 and took effect on 1 May 2022, replacing a 1995-era individual-secrets law. It was passed as part of a package with the Cybersecurity Law, Public Information Transparency Law and Electronic Signature Law, together forming Mongolia's first comprehensive digital-governance framework. The law applies to individuals, legal entities and organisations collecting, processing and using personal data in Mongolia, and is broadly consent-based, with heightened rules for sensitive categories including health, genetic and biometric data.

Distinctively, Mongolia has no dedicated data protection authority: compliance oversight sits with the National Human Rights Commission of Mongolia, while the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications handles digital-security aspects. There is no registration regime and no general DPO mandate. Sanctions are imposed under the general Law on Violations, with fines ranging from roughly MNT 500,000 to MNT 20,000,000 (about USD 150–5,800) depending on the offence.

Enforcement is still maturing — the NHRC's role is closer to a human-rights ombudsman than an inspecting regulator, and practice on issues like breach handling and cross-border transfers (generally consent-based) is thin. Businesses operating in Mongolia should anchor compliance in documented consent, purpose limitation, security measures for sensitive data, and the specific rules on workplace monitoring and CCTV that the law introduced.

summary: Montenegro still operates under its pre-GDPR Personal Data Protection Law of 2008 (Official Gazette 79/08 and 70/09), amended several times since — most recently in July 2024. The law follows the old EU Directive 95/46 model: it applies to controllers processing personal data in Montenegro, requires a legal basis for processing, obliges controllers to register their data filing systems with the supervisory Agency, and channels most enforcement through a misdemeanour-fine regime with maximum penalties of only EUR 20,000 for legal entities.

Supervision sits with the Agency for Personal Data Protection and Free Access to Information (AZLP), which handles both data protection and freedom-of-information. Cross-border transfers to countries lacking adequate protection require the Agency's approval, and there is no general data breach notification duty — hallmarks of the framework's age. Enforcement is real but low-stakes by European standards, and the European Commission has repeatedly flagged that the law is not aligned with the GDPR or the Law Enforcement Directive.

A comprehensive GDPR-aligned replacement law has been in the works for years as part of Montenegro's EU accession (Chapter 23). In March 2026 the Ministry of Interior submitted the draft new Law on Personal Data Protection to the European Commission for review, but as of August 2026 it has not been adopted by Parliament. Anyone doing business in Montenegro should comply with the 2008 law today while preparing for a GDPR-style overhaul in the near term. Note that some secondary trackers incorrectly report a 2023 GDPR-aligned act as already in force — official and law-firm sources confirm the 2008 law remains the one in effect.

summary: Morocco's Law 09-08, promulgated in February 2009, was one of the first comprehensive data protection statutes in North Africa and is closely modeled on the pre-GDPR European Directive 95/46/EC. summary: The Netherlands is governed directly by the EU GDPR, supplemented by the national GDPR Implementation Act (Uitvoeringswet AVG, or UAVG), both effective 25 May 2018. The UAVG fills in the areas where the GDPR leaves member states discretion — for example retaining the default age of 16 for children's online consent and setting rules for processing national identification numbers (BSN), which may only be used where a statute specifically permits it. The framework applies to any organisation established in the Netherlands and to foreign organisations targeting or monitoring people there.

The regulator, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP) in The Hague, is one of Europe's more active authorities. It has issued some of the EU's largest fines — including a €290 million penalty against Uber in 2024 over unlawful transfers of driver data to the US — and publishes extensive Dutch-language guidance on cookies, algorithms and AI. The AP also serves as one of the Netherlands' coordinating regulators for the EU AI Act, making it a key interlocutor for companies deploying automated decision-making.

Practically, Dutch compliance is standard GDPR compliance: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs for high-risk processing, and DPO appointment where Art. 37 thresholds are met. The main Dutch-specific traps are strict BSN rules, the AP's assertive position on tracking cookies and legitimate-interest advertising, and active private litigation including collective actions under Dutch class-action law.

Law 2022-59 is now Niger's principal, comprehensive data protection statute, and the country therefore remains in the 'law in force' category — but citations should point to the 2022 Act.

The supervisory authority is the Haute Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (HAPDP). The 2022 Act introduced modern elements including a mandatory breach-notification duty: under Article 83, controllers must inform the HAPDP without delay upon becoming aware of a breach, and must inform data subjects as soon as possible where there is high risk to their rights and freedoms. Notably, the law contains no DPO appointment requirement. Non-compliance with obligations, including breach notification, is backed by criminal penalties (imprisonment and fines) under Article 98.

Enforcement reality is shaped by Niger's post-July 2023 political situation: the HAPDP has continued operating, with commentary through 2024 describing an authority balancing awareness-raising against control activity. Practical enforcement remains light, and detailed transfer and penalty specifics under the 2022-59/2023-31 framework are not well documented in accessible public sources.

summary: North Korea (DPRK) has no data protection or privacy law in any recognizable sense, and no supervisory authority. The state operates one of the world's most pervasive surveillance systems: personal information is collected and used by the state for control purposes, and there are no independent bodies, judicial remedies or legal mechanisms through which citizens could challenge the handling of their data.

The legislation that does touch information is oriented toward state control rather than individual rights — for example, the Law on Protection of State Secrets adopted in 2023, which criminalizes leakage of classified information and further restricts citizens' access to and dissemination of information. Enforcement is carried out by the Ministry of State Security without oversight, with penalties that can include imprisonment, forced labour or execution.

For any organization, the question of DPRK data compliance is academic: foreign businesses do not process North Korean personal data under local law, and comprehensive international sanctions bar most commercial activity. There is no constitutional or statutory privacy protection with practical effect, no DPO, registration, breach or transfer rules, and no realistic prospect of data protection legislation.

summary: North Macedonia's Law on Personal Data Protection (Official Gazette No. 42/2020, amended by 294/21) took effect on 24 February 2020 and is a close transposition of the EU GDPR, adopted as part of the country's EU accession agenda. After an 18-month transition, it has been fully applicable since August 2021. It covers controllers and processors on Macedonian territory and adopts GDPR concepts wholesale: legal bases, data subject rights, records of processing, DPIAs, and privacy by design.

The old general database registration requirement from the 2005 law was scrapped — the Agency's Central Registry survives only for high-risk databases, which controllers must notify. DPOs are mandatory for public bodies and for organisations doing large-scale systematic monitoring or extensive special-category processing. Breaches must be reported to the Agency within 72 hours unless unlikely to pose a risk to individuals.

Enforcement is handled by the Agency for Personal Data Protection (AZLP) in Skopje, an independent state body with inspection and sanctioning powers. Fines mirror the GDPR's turnover-based logic — up to 4% of a company's total annual income of the preceding financial year, with additional personal fines of EUR 300–500 for responsible officers. In practice the Agency is active on complaints and inspections, though headline fines remain far smaller than in EU member states.

summary: Norway applies the full text of the EU GDPR through the EEA Agreement, incorporated by the Personal Data Act of 15 June 2018 (personopplysningsloven), which entered into force on 20 July 2018. The Act fills the gaps the GDPR leaves to national law — for example on the digital age of consent (13), employment-related processing and exemptions — but the substantive regime is the GDPR itself, applying to any organisation established in Norway or targeting people there.

The supervisory authority, Datatilsynet, is one of Europe's more assertive enforcers relative to market size, with a record that includes the landmark Grindr fine over unlawful sharing of user data with advertisers, and firm positions on tracking, cloud services and workplace monitoring. Because Norway sits outside the EU institutional framework, Datatilsynet participates in the European Data Protection Board without voting rights, but applies EDPB guidance in practice.

As an EEA state inside the GDPR zone, Norway needs no EU adequacy decision — personal data flows freely between Norway and EU member states, and transfers out of the EEA follow the standard GDPR Chapter V toolkit.

summary: Poland is governed by the EU GDPR, supplemented by the Act of 10 May 2018 on the Protection of Personal Data, which took effect on 25 May 2018 and replaced the 1997 act. The 2018 Act contains few substantive derogations from the GDPR: its main role is establishing the supervisory authority (UODO, replacing the former GIODO), setting procedural rules for inspections and administrative proceedings, capping fines on public bodies at PLN 100,000, and retaining the GDPR default age of 16 for children's online consent. A companion 'sectoral implementation' act of 2019 amended over 160 other statutes, including significant employer rules on employee monitoring and recruitment data.

The President of UODO is appointed by the Sejm for a four-year term and runs an active enforcement programme: annual inspection plans, published decisions, and fines against both private companies and public institutions. Decisions can be appealed to the administrative courts, which have overturned several UODO fines, so enforcement is genuinely contested.

In practice, compliance in Poland is standard GDPR work — lawful basis, transparency in Polish, 72-hour breach reporting, DPIAs against UODO's published high-risk list — with local specifics around employee monitoring notice requirements and the obligation to notify DPO appointments to UODO electronically.

summary: Portugal applies the GDPR directly, executed nationally by Law No. 58/2019 of 8 August. The national law sets the digital consent age at 13 — the lowest the GDPR permits — and requires that parental consent for younger children be collected through secure authentication means such as the Citizen's Card. It also contains Portuguese specifics on employee data, health data, deceased persons' data, and video surveillance, and structures fines into national bands within GDPR ceilings.

Supervision belongs to the CNPD (Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados). A notable quirk: shortly after Law 58/2019 passed, the CNPD publicly deliberated that it would disapply several of its provisions it considered incompatible with the GDPR's primacy — so practitioners rely on the GDPR text over the national law where they conflict. The law also allowed public entities a temporary waiver from fines, reflecting a historically softer enforcement posture toward the public sector.

Enforcement has grown steadily, with the CNPD issuing fines on video surveillance, municipalities and data-subject-rights failures, and intervening prominently on international transfers (notably ordering suspension of transfers in the Census 2021 Cloudflare case). Day-to-day compliance is standard GDPR with the age-13 rule and secure parental authentication as Portuguese distinctives.

summary: Romania is an EU member state where the GDPR applies directly, supplemented by Law No. 190/2018 (in force 31 July 2018). The national law adds conditions for processing national identification numbers (CNP), genetic, biometric and health data, workplace monitoring rules, and a distinctive lighter-touch regime for public authorities: ANSPDCP first issues a warning and a remediation plan, and fines on public bodies are capped at RON 200,000.

The framework also includes Law No. 102/2005 establishing the supervisory authority, Law No. 363/2018 transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, and Law No. 506/2004 on ePrivacy in electronic communications. The authority, ANSPDCP, is an autonomous body based in Bucharest that issues secondary regulations on DPIAs, breach reporting and certification.

Workplace monitoring is a notable Romanian specificity: employee monitoring via electronic means or CCTV requires a legitimate-interest justification, prior consultation, and is only allowed if less intrusive methods have not proven effective. Enforcement is regular though fines are typically modest compared with Western European authorities.

summary: Russia's Federal Law No. 152-FZ 'On Personal Data', enacted in 2006, is a comprehensive consent-centric regime that has been amended repeatedly and now anchors one of the world's most restrictive data governance systems. It applies to any 'operator' processing personal data of Russian citizens, and its most distinctive features are mandatory data localization (databases with Russians' personal data must be located in Russia — a rule tightened from 1 July 2025 to cover processors as well), mandatory notification of Roskomnadzor before processing begins, and a separate prior notification before any cross-border transfer, with transfers to some jurisdictions subject to restriction.

Enforcement has hardened sharply since 2022. Breaches must be reported to Roskomnadzor within 24 hours (with a 72-hour detailed follow-up). Federal Law 420-FZ, in force since 30 May 2025, introduced turnover-based fines: data leaks now attract fines of RUB 3–15 million depending on the number of affected individuals, and repeat leak violations can cost up to 3% of annual turnover, capped at RUB 500 million. Parallel Federal Law 421-FZ created criminal liability — up to four years' imprisonment — for illegal collection, use or transfer of personal data, with harsher sentences involving minors' or biometric data.

Roskomnadzor is an assertive regulator with website-blocking powers (LinkedIn has been blocked since 2016 over localization). Russia holds no EU adequacy decision, so GDPR-covered transfers into Russia require safeguards, while outbound compliance for foreign companies serving Russian users is dominated by localization, notification and consent formalities.

summary: Rwanda's Law No. 058/2021 on the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy (in force since 15 October 2021, with a two-year transition that ended 15 October 2023) is one of Africa's most GDPR-aligned and operationally serious regimes. It applies to controllers and processors in Rwanda and to those abroad processing data of people in Rwanda. Supervision sits with the Data Protection and Privacy Office of the National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA), which runs an active registration system, publishes guidance, and issued standard contractual clauses for transfers in February 2024.

Several features are stricter than the GDPR: breaches must be notified to the NCSA within 48 hours (not 72); registration as a controller or processor is mandatory; a DPO is required for sensitive or large-scale processing; children under 16 need parental consent; and cross-border transfers require NCSA authorization with proven safeguards, consent, or a narrow necessity exception — layered on top of a national policy preference that data be hosted in Rwanda unless approved otherwise. Sanctions combine administrative fines (up to RWF 5 million or 1% of global turnover) with criminal penalties that can reach 5% of turnover and imprisonment.

Enforcement reality: the NCSA is regarded as one of the more capable regulators in the region, registration campaigns have had firm deadlines, and Rwanda's positioning as a digital/financial hub (Kigali International Financial Centre) gives compliance genuine commercial weight. Foreign companies serving Rwandan users should assume the law applies extraterritorially and that registration and transfer approvals will be checked.

summary: San Marino's Law No. 171 of 21 December 2018 is a comprehensive data protection statute closely modelled on the GDPR — it reproduces the Regulation's principles, lawful bases, data subject rights, accountability obligations and breach-notification regime. A consolidated text incorporating amendments through 2023 is published by the Great and General Council and by the supervisory authority.

The law established an independent supervisory authority, the Autorità Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali, a collegial body of three members supported by an office. It holds investigative, corrective, authorisation and advisory powers, including the distinctive ability to grant an infringer a deadline of up to six months to come into compliance before or alongside sanctions (Article 73). Controllers must notify personal data breaches presenting risk to individuals without undue delay and, where possible, within 72 hours.

Despite its GDPR-inspired framework, San Marino does not hold an EU adequacy decision, so EEA organisations transferring data to San Marino still need Chapter V safeguards. Enforcement activity is modest and mostly guidance-oriented, consistent with the microstate's size.

summary: São Tomé & Príncipe enacted Law No. 03/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data as its general data protection framework. The law is closely modeled on the EU's former Data Protection Directive (95/46/EC) and Portugal's Act 67/98, so its architecture will feel familiar to anyone who worked with pre-GDPR European law: consent or another legal ground for processing, prior notification to the regulator (with authorization for sensitive data), data quality principles, and adequacy-based rules for international transfers.

The supervisory authority, the Agência Nacional de Protecção de Dados Pessoais (ANPDP), is a genuine bright spot for a small island state: it is operational and relatively active, issuing authorisations, resolutions and opinions, operating under the National Assembly as an independent administrative entity, and participating in regional networks (NADPA and the francophone AFAPDP). Entities must generally obtain data-subject consent and give prior notice to the ANPDP before collecting and processing personal data.

Because the law predates the GDPR, it lacks modern features — there is no general breach-notification duty, no DPO requirement, and no turnover-based fines — and detailed English-language documentation of penalty levels is sparse. For most international businesses exposure is limited, but anyone processing Santomean data at scale (telecoms, banking, the growing digital-government program) should file notifications with the ANPDP and track possible modernization of the 2016 framework.

summary: Senegal was one of Africa's data protection pioneers: Law No. 2008-12 of 25 January 2008 established a comprehensive regime and created the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles (CDP), one of the continent's first operational supervisory authorities. The law follows the pre-GDPR French/CNIL model — built around declarations and prior authorisations to the regulator rather than accountability tools like DPOs and breach notification.

Controllers must declare most processing to the CDP and obtain prior authorisation for sensitive categories such as biometric and genetic data, criminal records and national ID numbers. There is no mandatory breach-notification duty and DPO appointment is discretionary, which makes the regime feel dated next to newer African laws. Cross-border transfers are permitted only to countries offering 'sufficient protection', assessed by the CDP.

A modernising replacement bill — addressing biometrics, big data, AI and a strengthened authority — has been in preparation since 2019 under the Digital Senegal strategy, with a finalisation workshop held by the CDP and the digital ministry in October 2024, but it had not been adopted as of mid-2026, so the 2008 law remains in force. The CDP is active in awareness-raising and issues regular deliberations, though monetary enforcement has historically been light.

summary: Serbia's Law on Personal Data Protection (ZZPL), published in Official Gazette No. 87/2018 and applicable since August 2019, is closely modelled on the GDPR and unusually also incorporates the EU Law Enforcement Directive in the same statute. It brings GDPR-style principles, data subject rights, accountability tools (records, DPIAs, DPOs), 72-hour breach notification and extraterritorial reach over foreign controllers targeting people in Serbia. Serbia set the child consent age for information society services at 15.

The supervisory authority is the Poverenik — the Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection — a well-established independent body that also handles freedom of information. The law's biggest weakness is its misdemeanour-based sanctions: fines are capped at RSD 2 million (roughly €17,000), far below GDPR levels, which limits deterrence even as inspection activity increases.

Reform is underway: the Government adopted a Personal Data Protection Strategy 2023–2030, and in January 2025 a working group began drafting ZZPL amendments to cover gaps such as cookies, video surveillance, biometrics and AI. As of August 2026 the 2018 law remains in force and the amendment timeline is uncertain. Serbia does not hold an EU adequacy decision; cross-border transfers are free to Convention 108 parties and listed adequate countries, with safeguards or Commissioner approval otherwise.

summary: Seychelles' Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023) was gazetted and entered into force on 22 December 2023, replacing the Data Protection Act 2003 — a law that had been enacted but never brought into practical operation. The new Act is a modern, GDPR-influenced framework covering data controllers and processors, with duties around lawful processing, retention, security, cross-border transfers and the appointment of data protection officers for organisations of sufficient size or processing risk.

Supervision sits with the Information Commission, which also handles access to information; it is empowered to conduct audits and investigations and to impose administrative fines. Controllers must notify the Commission within 72 hours of discovering a breach that may put data subjects' rights and freedoms at risk, and children's data (under 18) may only be processed with parental or guardian consent.

All controllers and processors were given an 18-month transition from 22 December 2023, which expired in June 2025 — so the Act is now fully applicable. Enforcement history is still short, and no EU adequacy decision exists; businesses should track Information Commission guidance as its data protection practice develops.

summary: Sierra Leone still has no comprehensive data protection law, but the legislative process is well advanced. The Ministry of Information and Civic Education completed the final national validation of the Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill, 2025 in November 2025, after nationwide consultations involving Parliament, local councils, security agencies, the Electoral Commission, civil society, media, academia and the private sector.

In April 2026, Cabinet approved the country's first National Data Protection Policy and authorized drafting and enactment of a combined Data Protection and Right to Access Information Act — a distinctive design that would merge data protection and access-to-information functions into a single strengthened authority (building on the existing Right to Access Information Commission). The Ministry has been directed to work with the Attorney-General's office to finalize and table the Bill in Parliament.

As of August 2026 the Bill has not been enacted. The forthcoming law is expected to impose stricter protocols on banks, mobile network operators and government agencies over citizens' financial, digital, health and tax records, and to align Sierra Leone with international data standards for trade. In the meantime, protections rest on constitutional privacy rights and sectoral rules such as the Cyber Security and Crime Act, 2021.

summary: Slovakia applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by Act No. 18/2018 Coll. on the Protection of Personal Data, adopted 29 November 2017 and effective 25 May 2018. Unusually, the Act restates much of the GDPR's text verbatim in Slovak law (to cover processing outside the GDPR's scope and transpose the Law Enforcement Directive), while adding national derogations: it keeps the children's online consent age at 16, regulates processing of birth numbers and employee data disclosure, and sets procedural rules for the supervisory authority.

The Office for Personal Data Protection of the Slovak Republic (Úrad na ochranu osobných údajov SR) in Bratislava supervises compliance, conducts inspections under an annual plan, handles complaints, and issues decisions and methodological guidance. Enforcement is steady but fines are typically modest — usually in the thousands to tens of thousands of euros — with an emphasis on corrective measures.

Compliance is standard GDPR practice with Slovak specifics: transparency in Slovak, the 16-year consent age, restrictions on using the national birth number as an identifier, and a statutory rule allowing employers to disclose limited employee contact data. Because Act 18/2018 duplicates GDPR text, practitioners must track which provisions apply directly under the Regulation versus the national Act.

summary: Slovenia is an EU member state, so the GDPR has applied directly since May 2018. However, Slovenia was famously the last EU country to pass a national GDPR implementing act: the Personal Data Protection Act (ZVOP-2) was adopted in December 2022 and entered into force on 26 January 2023. Until then, the Information Commissioner could not impose GDPR administrative fines because Slovenia lacked the domestic procedural machinery; full and systematic enforcement has only been possible since ZVOP-2 took effect.

ZVOP-2 supplements the GDPR with national specifics: a consent age of 15 for children in information society services, detailed data-security duties including traceability logs for certain processing, rules on video surveillance and biometrics, and localised fine provisions enforced through the fast-track misdemeanour procedure. The Information Commissioner (IP-RS) is a well-regarded, active authority that also handles freedom-of-information matters.

For anyone doing business in Slovenia, compliance is essentially GDPR compliance plus the ZVOP-2 national add-ons. Enforcement has stepped up markedly since 2023, with the IP-RS now conducting audits and imposing fines directly.

summary: Somalia enacted its first comprehensive privacy statute, the Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023), signed by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on 21 March 2023 and effective from 23 March 2023. Modeled in significant part on modern African frameworks such as Nigeria's NDPA, it regulates collection, storage, processing and transfer of personal data across all sectors, and scales obligations by imposing the heaviest duties on 'controllers and processors of major importance'.

The Somali Data Protection Authority (DPA) was officially launched in February 2024 and is unusually active for a young regulator — publishing guidance, implementing regulations and e-services. Key obligations include 72-hour breach notification to the Authority, DPO appointment for government bodies and larger or sensitive-data processors, adequacy-or-safeguards rules for cross-border transfers, and parental consent for data of children under 18.

Penalties can reach a percentage (commentators cite 2–4%) of annual turnover, though enforcement is still building and implementing regulations continue to flesh out the regime. Somalia has no EU adequacy decision; the practical compliance picture depends heavily on DPA guidance.

summary: South Sudan has no data protection law and no supervisory authority, but the picture is moving. The government announced that its first-ever Data Protection Bill would be introduced in 2026, to be drafted jointly by the ministries of information and justice as part of a push to have all cyberspace-governing laws in place — though as of August 2026 no tabled bill or published draft could be verified.

The country's flagship digital statute is instead the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, signed by President Salva Kiir on 18 February 2026 and now being enforced ahead of the December 2026 elections. It criminalises online fraud, harassment and harmful content, and includes some data-related offences, but it is a criminal statute — press-freedom groups including CPJ have warned it threatens journalists — not a data protection regime conferring rights on data subjects.

Beyond that, protections are limited to the constitutional right to privacy in the Transitional Constitution and scattered sectoral provisions. Organizations handling South Sudanese data face no domestic registration, DPO or breach duties today, but should watch for the promised Data Protection Bill later in 2026.

summary: Spain applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD), which goes further than most member-state laws: beyond filling GDPR opening clauses it adds a catalogue of "digital rights" — digital disconnection at work, device privacy for employees, digital education, and rights concerning deceased persons' data. The digital consent age is set at 14, and Article 34 makes DPO appointment mandatory for 16 listed sectors (including banks, insurers, health centres, schools, telecoms and gambling operators) regardless of size, with appointments notified to the AEPD within 10 days.

The regulator is the AEPD, consistently among the most active supervisory authorities in Europe by volume of resolutions and fines, with major penalties against banks, telecoms and utilities. Spain also uses statutory presumptions (e.g. blocklist rules, video surveillance and workplace monitoring provisions in the LOPDGDD) that give enforcement a distinctly codified flavour compared with other member states.

Compliance is standard GDPR — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, Chapter V transfers — plus the Spanish extras: check whether your sector triggers mandatory DPO designation, honour employees' digital rights, and apply the age-14 rule for minors' consent.

summary: Sudan has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. A Draft Data Protection Bill was proposed in 2018 to set out rules for the collection, storage, processing and sharing of personal information, but it never advanced to enactment, and the legislative process has been effectively frozen — first by the 2021 coup and then by the civil war that broke out in April 2023 and was still ongoing as of 2026.

What exists instead is a patchwork of sectoral instruments: the Electronic Transactions Act 2007, the Cybercrime Act 2007 and the Cybercrime Prevention (Amendment) Act 2020, plus informational-crimes provisions. These laws criminalize certain misuse of computer systems and communications but do not create data-subject rights, controller obligations, or a supervisory regime. Constitutional privacy guarantees under the 2019 Constitutional Document are of limited practical effect given the collapse of transitional institutions.

For any organization handling Sudanese personal data, the practical position is that there are no registration, DPO, breach-notification or transfer rules to comply with domestically — but also no legal certainty. Expect no near-term movement on a data protection statute while the conflict continues.

summary: As an EU member state, Sweden is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented by the Data Protection Act (2018:218) — 'the Act with supplementary provisions to the EU GDPR' (dataskyddslagen) — and the Data Protection Ordinance (2018:219), both in force since 25 May 2018. The national law exercises GDPR opening clauses, setting the digital age of consent at 13, regulating personal identity numbers, and preserving Sweden's strong constitutional protections for freedom of expression and press, which carve journalistic and constitutionally protected publishing out of much of the regime.

The supervisory authority is IMY (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten, the Swedish Authority for Privacy Protection), renamed from the Data Inspection Board (Datainspektionen) in January 2021. Sweden has one of the world's oldest data protection traditions — its first national data act dates to 1973 — and IMY actively audits, handles complaints and issues administrative fines, with a distinctive national cap of SEK 10 million for fines against public authorities.

Compliance for organisations operating in Sweden is essentially GDPR compliance: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, and Chapter V safeguards for transfers outside the EU/EEA.

summary: Switzerland's fully revised Federal Act on Data Protection (revFADP), adopted in September 2020 and in force since 1 September 2023, modernised Swiss law to GDPR-comparable standards while keeping a distinctly Swiss design. It applies to private controllers and federal bodies, has extraterritorial effect on processing with effects in Switzerland, and requires foreign companies meeting thresholds to appoint a Swiss representative. The EU renewed Switzerland's adequacy status on 15 January 2024, so EU-Swiss data flows remain free.

The headline structural difference from the GDPR is sanctions: there are no corporate administrative fines. Instead, intentional violations of specific duties (information, disclosure, security, transfer rules) are criminal offences punishable by fines up to CHF 250,000 imposed on responsible individuals — managers, not companies — which changes personal risk calculations for executives. Breach notification runs to the FDPIC "as soon as possible" only where high risk is involved, and a DPO ("data protection advisor") is optional.

Compliance staples include records of processing (with an exemption for companies under 250 employees and low-risk processing), privacy by design and default, DPIAs for high-risk processing, and transfer checks against the Federal Council's country adequacy list. The FDPIC supervises and investigates but cannot itself levy fines; prosecution runs through cantonal criminal authorities.

summary: Syria has no comprehensive data protection or privacy law, and no bill for one is known to be in progress as of August 2026. Privacy protections are fragmentary: the Constitutional Declaration of 13 March 2025, issued by the transitional government after the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, contains general rights guarantees, and older sectoral rules (telecommunications regulation, banking secrecy, and general civil/criminal provisions on correspondence and defamation) provide narrow, uneven coverage.

The closest thing to data-related legislation is the Assad-era Cybercrime Law No. 20 of 2022, which criminalises certain misuse of information systems and online content but is primarily a speech-control instrument, with vague offences such as 'undermining the prestige of the state'. Human rights organisations — including Amnesty International and the Syrian Network for Human Rights — have documented its continued use by transitional authorities against journalists and activists through 2026. In June 2026 the Ministry of Justice announced a review of the law to harmonise it with the Constitutional Declaration and international standards, and introduced some limits on its use, but it remains in force.

For any organisation handling Syrian personal data, the practical position is that there is no supervisory authority, no registration, breach-notification or transfer regime, and no data-subject rights framework. Compliance decisions should be driven by the laws of the organisation's own jurisdiction (e.g. GDPR for EU entities), sanctions considerations, and heightened ethical duties of care given the acute risks that data exposure poses to individuals in Syria's transitional context.

summary: Tanzania's Personal Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 11 of 2022, passed 27 November 2022, in force 1 May 2023) established the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) and, together with the May 2023 Regulations on collection/processing and complaints handling, created a complete operative regime. The framework's defining feature is gatekeeping: controllers and processors must register with the PDPC before processing any personal data, and cross-border transfers require a prior PDPC permit backed by adequacy findings, international or bilateral agreements, or contractual safeguards.

Obligations include appointing a data protection officer, notifying the Commission of security breaches without undue delay, and observing GDPR-style processing principles and data subject rights. Sanctions are layered: administrative enforcement and penalty notices up to TZS 100 million plus uncapped compensation orders, and criminal offences (such as unlawful disclosure) carrying fines up to TZS 5 billion for corporates and up to 10 years' imprisonment for individuals.

Enforcement has moved from theory to practice quickly. Registration deadlines were extended through 2025, with the PDPC signaling full enforcement against unregistered processors from April 2026; the Commission has also begun issuing substantive decisions — notably a 2025 ruling that children's images are sensitive personal data whose commercial use without parental consent is unlawful. Any business touching Tanzanian personal data in 2026 should treat registration, DPO appointment and transfer permits as immediate, actively-policed requirements.

summary: Togo's Law No. 2019-014 of 29 October 2019 is a GDPR-inspired framework governing the collection, processing, transmission, storage and use of personal data. It rests on principles of consent and legitimacy, lawfulness, accuracy, transparency, confidentiality and security, and applies broadly to public and private controllers processing data in Togo. Outside limited exemptions, processing must be declared in advance to the supervisory authority, which issues a receipt; transfers of data abroad require the authority's authorization.

The supervisory authority, the Instance de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (IPDCP), took years to materialise: its president, Lt-Col Bédiani Béléi, was appointed by presidential decree in September 2024 and the authority was officially launched on 28 March 2025. It is now standing up its operational committees, running awareness campaigns and beginning to accompany businesses and administrations toward compliance — so active enforcement is only just starting.

Violations can attract fines up to XOF 10 million and/or prison terms of up to five years. Togo has no EU adequacy decision; practitioners should watch for IPDCP implementing decisions and compliance formalities now that the regulator is live.

summary: Tunisia was the first Arab country to adopt comprehensive data protection legislation: Organic Act No. 2004-63 of 27 July 2004, which establishes general principles of lawful processing, data subject rights, and the independent supervisory authority, the INPDP. The regime rests on prior formalities — declarations to the INPDP before processing, with authorizations needed for certain categories — and treats children's data with unusual care, involving guardian consent and judicial oversight.

The 2004 Act is now widely regarded as outdated, and a full replacement is in progress. A GDPR-inspired organic bill of 123 articles — covering processing principles, data subject rights (including portability and erasure), a strengthened supervisory authority, high-risk processing rules relevant to AI, and deterrent sanctions — was under examination by the Rights and Freedoms Committee of the Assembly of People's Representatives as of early 2026, but had not been reported as finally adopted.

In practice, enforcement under the 2004 Act relies on criminal-style penalties rather than large administrative fines, and the INPDP has historically been more visible in advocacy and opinions than in heavy sanctions. Businesses meeting professionals should assume the 2004 declaration regime applies today while planning for a significantly stricter GDPR-style law once the pending bill passes.

summary: Turkey's Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data (KVKK), in force since 2016, was modelled on the pre-GDPR EU Directive but was substantially modernised by the March 2024 amendments (Law 7499, the '8th Judicial Reform Package'), effective June 2024. The law applies to anyone processing personal data of individuals in Turkey and is enforced by the Personal Data Protection Authority and its decision-making Board in Ankara.

Turkey's most distinctive feature is VERBIS, the mandatory public registry of data controllers: Turkish controllers above employee/turnover thresholds and all foreign controllers processing Turkish personal data must register and appoint a contact person (Turkey does not mandate a GDPR-style DPO). The 2024 reform overhauled the previously restrictive cross-border transfer regime — which had effectively required explicit consent or Board permission — replacing it with a GDPR-like structure of adequacy decisions, Turkish Standard Contractual Clauses (which must be filed with the Authority within five business days of signing), and Binding Corporate Rules. It also expanded the legal bases for processing sensitive data, notably for employment purposes.

Enforcement is vigorous and fines are indexed annually for inflation: 2026 amounts reach TRY 17,092,242 per violation, with VERBIS failures alone drawing fines from TRY 341,809 upward. Breach notification to the Board is due within 72 hours under Board decision 2019/10, plus notification to affected individuals. Multinationals should treat Turkey as a distinct compliance regime — GDPR compliance helps but does not cover VERBIS registration, Turkish-language SCC filing, or local sensitive-data rules.

summary: Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 (now Cap. 97) is one of East Africa's established regimes, fleshed out by the Data Protection and Privacy Regulations, 2021. It applies to anyone collecting or processing personal data of Ugandan residents — including offshore entities, as the regulator clarified in 2025 guidance — and is supervised by the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO), an office established under NITA-U that has grown into an active regulator.

The regime is registration-heavy: every data collector, processor and controller must register with the PDPO through its online portal, and registration must be renewed annually — failure to register is itself an offence. Cross-border transfers are permitted only with the data subject's consent or where the receiving jurisdiction provides protection at least equivalent to the Act, and controllers must keep records justifying each transfer for inspection.

Enforcement has moved from theory to practice, with the PDPO issuing registration decisions, its first fines, and Uganda recording criminal data protection convictions in 2025. Corporate offenders face fines up to 2% of annual gross turnover on conviction, alongside individual fines and potential imprisonment. Uganda holds no EU adequacy decision.

summary: Ukraine's framework is still the Law on Personal Data Protection No. 2297-VI, adopted on 1 June 2010 and in force since 1 January 2011. It is a pre-GDPR, Convention 108-style law applying to controllers and processors handling personal data of individuals in Ukraine. Since 2014 supervision has sat with the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman) rather than a dedicated data protection authority — an unusual arrangement the pending reform would end.

The law requires a legal basis for processing, notification of high-risk processing to the Ombudsman, designation of a responsible person for such processing, and observance of data subject rights. Enforcement is real but light: the Ombudsman investigates complaints and conducts inspections, but fines under the Code of Administrative Offences top out around UAH 34,000 (under EUR 1,000), so reputational and criminal exposure matter more than administrative penalties.

The big story is reform: Draft Law No. 8153 passed its first reading on 20 November 2024 and, as of mid-2026, remains in preparation for a second reading. It would align Ukraine with the GDPR and Convention 108+, create an independent supervisory authority, add 72-hour breach notification and DPO duties, and introduce fines up to UAH 150 million or 8% of annual turnover. EU accession pressure makes eventual adoption likely, so anyone building compliance in Ukraine should plan against GDPR-grade requirements.

summary: Post-Brexit, the UK runs a retained-EU-law regime: the UK GDPR (the EU GDPR as domesticated) together with the Data Protection Act 2018 and PECR. This framework is now being amended — not replaced — by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA), which received Royal Assent on 19 June 2025 and is being commenced in phases through June 2026, with a major tranche of data protection provisions in force from 5 February 2026. DUAA introduces 'recognised legitimate interests', relaxed rules on some cookies and on automated decision-making, a new statutory complaints-handling duty on controllers (from June 2026), and restructures the ICO into an 'Information Commission'.

The regime applies to any organisation established in the UK or targeting people there. The ICO is a globally prominent regulator that supervises via audits, enforcement notices and fines of up to £17.5 million or 4% of worldwide turnover; most controllers must pay an annual data protection fee, which funds the office. The digital age of consent is 13, reinforced by the ICO's influential Age Appropriate Design (Children's) Code.

Crucially for international business, the European Commission renewed the UK's two adequacy decisions on 19 December 2025 — after concluding the DUAA keeps UK protection 'essentially equivalent' to EU standards — so personal data continues to flow freely between the EU/EEA and the UK until 27 December 2031.

summary: Uzbekistan's Law No. ZRU-547 'On Personal Data', adopted 2 July 2019 and in force since 1 October 2019, is the country's first comprehensive data protection statute. It applies to state bodies and private operators alike, requires consent or another legal basis for processing, and obliges most operators to register their personal data databases with the Personalization Agency under the Ministry of Justice — a notification-style filing decided within 15 days, with exemptions for employment data, publicly available data and several other categories. Operators must also designate a responsible person or unit for data protection.

The law became internationally notorious for its 2021 data localization amendment, which required personal data of Uzbek citizens processed via information technologies to be stored on servers physically located in Uzbekistan, enforced through a special register and website blocking (applied at times to major foreign platforms). That regime was substantially dismantled by amendments in force from 27 March 2026: storage and processing abroad is now permitted provided information security requirements and international data protection standards are met, clearing the path for cross-border digital services.

Enforcement is administered by the Personalization Agency alongside telecom inspection bodies, with penalties that are modest in monetary terms (base-calculation-value fines and possible criminal liability) but operationally significant through blocking powers. For foreign businesses the practical agenda is database registration, appointing a responsible person, and tracking the new 2026 cross-border conditions.

summary: Zambia's Data Protection Act, 2021 (Act No. 3 of 2021) is a GDPR-influenced statute with a distinctly strict local flavor: it imposes mandatory registration of controllers and processors, mandatory DPO appointment, a 24-hour breach-notification window (among the world's tightest), and hard data-localization rules — sensitive personal data must be stored and processed inside Zambia, and even non-sensitive data can leave only with data-subject consent plus Commissioner-approved contracts, intragroup schemes, ministerial prescription or specific authorization. It applies extraterritorially to anyone processing the personal data of people in Zambia.

For several years the law outpaced its institutions — a Commissioner was appointed in 2023 but the office wasn't functional. That changed decisively: the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) is now fully operational, launched an online registration portal at dataprotection.gov.zm, and set a registration deadline of 30 April 2025, with non-registration punishable by a ZMW 200,000 fine and/or up to five years' imprisonment. General penalties scale to 2% of annual turnover for bodies corporate.

Practically, 2025–2026 marks Zambia's shift from legislative intent to regulatory action. Businesses — including foreign SaaS, fintech and telecom providers serving Zambian users — should confirm ODPC registration, appoint a DPO, map where sensitive data is hosted (localization is the most commercially disruptive requirement), and build 24-hour breach response into incident plans.

summary: Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07], enacted in December 2021 and effective from 11 March 2022, is a hybrid statute combining cybercrime offences with a data protection regime. The Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ) doubles as the Data Protection Authority. The Act covers lawful processing, data security, sensitive data, breach notification and cross-border transfers, though its data-subject rights are narrower than the GDPR's.

The regime hardened considerably with Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024 (Cyber and Data Protection — Licensing of Data Controllers and Appointment of Data Protection Officers — Regulations), promulgated 13 September 2024. Every data controller must obtain a data protection licence from POTRAZ (applications were due within six months, by 12 March 2025) and appoint a POTRAZ-certified DPO. Breach notification is unusually tight: 24 hours to POTRAZ, with high-risk breaches communicated to affected individuals within 72 hours.

Enforcement reality: POTRAZ has been actively driving licensing and DPO certification since 2024–25, making Zimbabwe one of the more operationally demanding regimes in the region.
